Five: if a survivor is a false friend, drop morphology and go to context. Six: after about thirty seconds, guess from connotation, flag it and move on.
cards.n: The order matters. Charge is the cheapest test and kills the most choices, so it goes first.
x: charge, part of speech, root, context, guess

cards.q: Because the evidence rested on a single blurry photograph, the prosecutor case was ______. Work through corroborated, tenuous, meticulous, prescient.
cards.a: The clue is negative, so corroborated (co- plus robor, strength), meticulous and prescient all go. The blank follows "was" and needs an adjective, which tenuous is. Tenu means thin: thin evidence. The answer is tenuous, in about twelve seconds.
cards.h: → eliminate, then confirm with the root
cards.n: Notice that three choices died on charge alone and the root was only needed to confirm the survivor.

cards.q: The fee is merely ______ — a few cents per transaction. Work through nominal, negligible, detrimental, punitive.
cards.a: Detrimental and punitive die immediately on charge, because "merely a few cents" is minimizing. Morphology cannot separate nominal (in name only) from negligible (too small to count) — that is a meaning call. A fee that exists but barely matters is nominal.
cards.h: → what the method kills, and where it stops
cards.n: This is the honest limit of the technique: it got you to a coin flip in five seconds, and the last step still needs vocabulary.

cards.q: Why does the method check the grammatical slot before it uses the roots?
cards.a: Because the slot is faster and more certain. A blank after "the" needs a noun, and no amount of root knowledge changes that — so the suffix test removes choices at no cost before you spend attention on meaning.
cards.n: Every step of the method is ordered by cost. Do the free eliminations first and spend your thinking on what is left.
x: it is faster and more certain

cards.q: Mark each positive or negative: benevolent, obstreperous, eulogize, disparage, munificent, malfeasance, propitious, antipathy, ameliorate, deprecate.
cards.a: Positive: benevolent, eulogize, munificent, propitious, ameliorate. Negative: obstreperous, disparage, malfeasance, antipathy, deprecate.
cards.n: You should be able to do all ten in under fifteen seconds without knowing what four of them mean. That is the whole skill.

cards.q: Give the part of speech: substantiate, substantive, substantiation. Then ambivalence and ambivalent. Then rectify and rectitude.
cards.a: Verb, adjective, noun. Then noun and adjective. Then verb and noun.
cards.n: Same root, three slots. Form, Structure and Sense questions are built out of exactly this.

cards.q: Break down: circumspect, perspicacious, intractable, magnanimous, convoluted, desultory, equivocal, obfuscate.
cards.a: Circum (around) plus spec (look) is cautious. Per (thoroughly) plus spic (see) is keenly perceptive. In (not) plus tract (pull) plus -able is stubborn. Magn (great) plus anim (soul) is generous in spirit. Con (together) plus volut (roll) is twisted and overly complex. De (away) plus sult (jump) is aimless. Equi (equal) plus voc (voice) is ambiguous or evasive. Ob (over) plus fusc (dark) is to make unclear.
cards.n: Every one of these is two pieces you already know. Nothing here needs a dictionary.

cards.q: Which mean the opposite of what they look like: invaluable, indefensible, inflammable, incontrovertible, ingenuous?
cards.a: Invaluable (extremely valuable), inflammable (burns easily) and ingenuous (naive, not "not genuine"). Indefensible and incontrovertible mean exactly what they look like.
cards.h: → the three, and why the other two are safe
cards.n: Three out of five is roughly the rate at which in- lies. It is common enough that you check the root every time.

cards.q: What is the rule for learning roots so they survive to test day?
cards.a: Never learn a root without an example word attached. About fifteen a day, each one carried by a word you can actually picture, beats a long list learned bare.
cards.n: A root with no word attached is a fact you will not retrieve under time pressure. The word is the handle.

cards.q: What do you write in your review log when you miss a vocabulary question?
cards.a: The word and its breakdown. If the word has no useful breakdown, write "memorize" beside it and move on — some words simply have to be learned whole.
cards.h: → what to record, and the exception
cards.n: The exception is not a failure of the method. It is the method telling you which words it cannot help with.

cards.q: Name some words that simply have to be memorized whole.
cards.a: Eschew, loath, regale and belie. None of them yields anything useful to a prefix or a root.
cards.n: Keeping a short list of these is worth more than trying to force a breakdown that is not there.

cards.a: To state firmly as true, with no proof offered yet — verb, neutral. "The historian asserts that the treaty was doomed the day it was signed, then spends a whole chapter proving it."
cards.n: Assert is about confidence, not evidence: a writer can assert first and support later, and that gap is what questions test.

cards.a: To argue or maintain a position against opposition — verb, neutral. "Biologists who study the cave fish contend that losing eyesight saved energy rather than costing the species anything."
cards.n: This word carries a fight with it, since you contend against someone, while the same root also gives us contentious.

cards.a: To put something forward as a starting assumption — verb, neutral. "The paper posits a single migration across the land bridge, then tests that idea against the ages of the campsites."
cards.n: From Latin ponere, to place: you posit an idea the way you place a piece on a board, to see what follows from it.

cards.a: To claim wrongdoing before anything is proved — verb, negative. "The pamphlet alleged that the canal company had bribed three inspectors, though its author produced no records at all."
cards.n: This is the newspaper's safety word: printing that someone allegedly did it reports the accusation without endorsing it.

cards.a: The idea an argument starts from and builds on — noun, neutral. "Her whole proposal rests on one premise: that the river's flow will stay steady for the next fifty years."
cards.n: Knock this out and the conclusion falls with it, which is why reading questions ask what an argument assumes rather than what it says.

cards.a: To justify, or to give adequate grounds for — verb, neutral. "A single odd reading does not warrant throwing out the model, so the team repeated the measurement before changing anything."
cards.n: On the test this is usually the verb for the evidence being enough, and an unwarranted claim is one the data never earned.

cards.a: To confirm a claim with independent further evidence — verb, positive. "Tree-ring data corroborated the sailors' journals: the winter of 1601 really was the coldest in living memory."
cards.n: The confirmation has to come from somewhere else, a second witness or a second method, so repeating your own measurement does not count.

cards.a: To strengthen or prop up something already standing — verb, positive. "The new fossil bolsters the theory that feathers appeared long before flight, adding a fourth species to a very short list."
cards.n: Think of the pillow of the same name: this word takes an argument from weak to stronger, never from nothing to something.

cards.a: To confirm the soundness or accuracy of something — verb, positive. "Field trials validated the soil model, since the predicted and measured nitrogen levels matched within a few percent."
cards.n: This word tests a thing and finds it sound, while corroborate adds outside evidence to a claim; the test keeps the two apart.

cards.a: To clear of blame, or prove right after doubt — verb, positive. "Decades of ridicule ended when the seafloor was mapped, vindicating the geologist who had proposed drifting continents in 1912."
cards.n: There has to be an earlier accusation or doubt for this word to answer; with no such history, it is the wrong pick.

cards.a: To bear witness to, or serve as evidence of — verb, positive. "The worn stone steps attest to centuries of traffic through the abbey door, long before any records of it were kept."
cards.n: Watch the grammar the test uses: things attest to a fact, while people attest that something happened, and the root is testify.

cards.a: To quote or name a source in support of a point — verb, neutral. "The senator cited three studies on lead pipes, but none of them had examined a city anywhere near the size of hers."
cards.n: Naming a source is not the same as proving a point, and Command of Evidence questions ask whether the source does the job.

cards.a: To call on an authority, rule or idea for support — verb, neutral. "Defending his fence, the farmer invoked a property law from 1878 that nobody in the county had read in decades."
cards.n: What you invoke already carries weight of its own, a law or a precedent or a principle, so the force is borrowed rather than shown.

cards.a: To emphasize, or draw attention to — verb, neutral. "The blackout underscored how little of the grid could run without the one aging plant on the river."
cards.n: It is the printer's underline turned into a verb, and on the test it marks a detail the passage wants weighed, not a new claim.

cards.a: To argue publicly in favor of something — verb and noun, positive. "Nurses advocated for shorter shifts for years before the hospital finally agreed to rewrite its schedule."
cards.n: The stress moves with the meaning, AD-vuh-kut for the person and AD-vuh-kate for the act, and the person always argues for something.

cards.a: A person who argues in favor of an idea or plan — noun, neutral. "Proponents of the new dam point to steadier irrigation; its opponents count the villages that would go under water."
cards.n: The pro- at the front gives it away, and its exact opposite, opponent, sits one prefix away.

cards.a: To question or argue against the truth of — verb, negative. "Few geologists dispute the crater's age now, though the first estimate was argued over for twenty years."
cards.n: Questioning a claim does not settle anything, and the test cares about that difference in force.

cards.a: To answer an argument with opposing reasoning — verb, neutral. "She rebutted the cost estimate point by point, showing that each figure had counted the same labor twice."
cards.n: A rebuttal answers an argument; it does not automatically defeat it, which is the weaker job the test assigns this word.

cards.a: To say or show the opposite of — verb, negative. "The satellite record contradicts the ship logs: where the sailors reported open water, the images show solid ice."
cards.n: Two accounts can contradict each other without either being disproved, and the test often asks only that you notice the clash.

cards.a: To damage the standing or believability of — verb, negative. "A single forged photograph discredited the whole expedition, and later findings from the same team were ignored for years."
cards.n: This one goes after the source rather than the claim, which is why an attack on a person can be unfair and still work.

cards.a: Disagreement with a majority or official view — noun and verb, neutral. "One justice dissented, arguing in forty pages that the majority had read the statute backward."
cards.n: This disagreement is public and on the record, since a dissenting opinion is filed rather than muttered, and consensus is its opposite.

cards.a: A flaw in reasoning that makes an argument fail — noun, negative. "Treating one warm winter as proof of a trend is a fallacy, since a single year cannot show a direction."
cards.n: The problem is in the reasoning, not the facts: an argument can run from true premises to a conclusion they never support.

cards.a: To describe as larger or stronger than it is — verb, negative. "The press release overstated the drug's effect, turning a three-point improvement into a breakthrough."
cards.n: This is the classic trap answer in Command of Evidence, where the data are real but the sentence claims more than they show.

cards.a: To admit that something is true or exists — verb, neutral. "The report acknowledges the gaps in its rainfall data before drawing any conclusion from the unusually wet years."
cards.n: Admitting a fact costs an author nothing on its own, so watch for the but that follows, where the real claim sits.

cards.a: To admit a point you would rather not — verb, neutral. "Even the mill's defenders conceded that the river ran warmer downstream, though they blamed the hot summer for it."
cards.n: This is not surrender: a writer gives up one small point to keep the larger argument, so even and though cluster around it.

cards.a: To limit a statement so that it claims less — verb, neutral. "He qualified his forecast, saying the harvest would improve only if the rains arrived before the end of May."
cards.n: The test's sense is not being eligible for something; look for mostly, often and under these conditions doing the limiting.

cards.a: To avoid committing to a firm position — verb and noun, negative. "The witness hedged, saying the car might have been blue and that the light was poor at the time."
cards.n: The word comes from the shrub border, and a hedged claim leaves the speaker a gap to slip through if it turns out wrong.

cards.a: To take as true in advance of proof — verb, neutral. "Early mapmakers presumed a great southern continent, and drew its coastline before anyone had seen a mile of it."
cards.n: This word assumes and then acts on the assumption, and presumptuous, from the same root, is what happens when someone overreaches.

cards.a: Resting on guesswork rather than evidence — adjective, negative. "The chapter on the city's fall is frankly speculative, since no text from those years survives to tell us anything."
cards.n: In science writing this is not an insult; it flags an idea as untested, and the passage usually says what would test it.

cards.a: Believable enough to be taken seriously — adjective, positive. "The only credible account of the fire comes from a clerk who wrote his notes the same night."
cards.n: Keep this apart from credulous, which describes a person who believes too easily; the test likes to pair the two.

cards.a: Doubtful, either feeling doubt or deserving it — adjective, negative. "The ledger's dubious entries, all written in the same fresh ink, convinced the auditor that someone had copied them later."
cards.n: It runs in both directions, since a dubious source invites the feeling and a dubious reader has it, from the same root as doubt.

cards.a: Seeming reasonable, though not proved — adjective, neutral. "A dropped lantern is a plausible cause of the fire, but investigators never found one anywhere in the ruins."
cards.n: This is a low bar, saying only that a claim could be true, so a passage calling an idea plausible has not endorsed it.

cards.a: Able to be defended against objection — adjective, positive. "After a third failed replication, the original explanation was no longer tenable, and the lab withdrew it."
cards.n: It comes from holding a position the way an army holds ground, and the negative form, untenable, is far more common on the test.

cards.a: Having no basis in evidence or fact — adjective, negative. "Fears that the vaccine caused the outbreak were unfounded, since the cases had begun two weeks before the first dose."
cards.n: Read the foundation metaphor: the claim was never built on anything, which is not the same as having been disproved.

cards.a: Strong enough to force belief or attention — adjective, positive. "The pattern of matching coastlines is compelling, which is why the idea survived its first round of critics."
cards.n: The root is compel, to force, so such evidence pushes a reader toward a conclusion while still falling short of settling it.

cards.a: Settling a question beyond further doubt — adjective, positive. "Nothing found in the wreck was conclusive until a bell with the ship's name came up on the last dive."
cards.n: This sits above compelling and plausible in strength, which makes it the overstated wrong choice in most evidence questions.

cards.a: Based on observation or experiment — adjective, neutral. "The claim finally got empirical support when buoys began recording the current's speed all year round."
cards.n: It answers how you know, with measurement rather than theory or intuition, so it says where knowledge came from, not that it is right.

cards.a: Resting on scattered personal reports — adjective, negative. "The evidence for the remedy is anecdotal: a few dozen letters from grateful patients and no trial of any size."
cards.n: Such evidence is real, just weak and unsystematic, and the test almost always pairs it against empirical or statistical.

cards.a: General agreement across a group — noun, neutral. "The consensus among climate scientists formed slowly, over three decades of measurements from ice, ocean and air."
cards.n: Broad agreement is not unanimity and not proof, so a passage can report one and still record a few holdouts.

cards.a: To communicate or get across — verb, neutral. "The letters convey a homesickness the official dispatches never mention, though both were written the same week."
cards.n: The idea is transfer, as in a conveyor belt, so questions built on it ask what a detail carries to the reader.

cards.a: To express clearly and in order, in words — verb and adjective, positive. "She articulated what the committee had circled for an hour: the bridge could be repaired or replaced, not both."
cards.n: The root means joint, as in an articulated limb, so the idea is put together part by part until it can move.

cards.a: To make clear by explaining — verb, positive. "A single diagram elucidated the engine's timing better than the six pages of description that came before it."
cards.n: Hear the luc, light, inside it, the same root as lucid, so the act is shining light on something already there.

cards.a: To serve as a typical example of — verb, neutral. "The crumbling seawall exemplifies the problem the whole coast faces: defenses built for a calmer century."
cards.n: The move runs from one case to a category, so the test asks whether the case really is typical of what it is said to show.

cards.a: To mean or stand for exactly — verb, neutral. "In these tables an asterisk denotes a measurement taken before the instruments were replaced in 1994."
cards.n: Denotation is the dictionary meaning, the one you could look up, while its partner connote carries everything else.

cards.a: To suggest beyond the literal meaning — verb, neutral. "Cheap and inexpensive point to the same price, but cheap also connotes shoddy work and corners cut."
cards.n: Words in Context questions live here, since two choices can share a dictionary meaning and only one fits the passage's attitude.

cards.a: To suggest something without stating it — verb, neutral. "The author never says the expedition was doomed, but the list of missing supplies implies it on the first page."
cards.n: The writer does this and the reader infers; the test punishes the swap, so keep the direction of travel straight.

cards.a: To work out a conclusion from evidence — verb, neutral. "From the depth of the ash, the team inferred that the eruption had lasted at least three days."
cards.n: The work happens in the reader's head, from clue to conclusion, and an inference question asks what follows, not what is said.

cards.a: To find out for certain by checking — verb, neutral. "Divers could not ascertain the hull's condition until the silt settled, two days after the storm passed."
cards.n: The certain sitting inside it is the hook, and it rules out guessing: the fact is established, not supposed.

cards.q: The lab's first result looked strange, but two other teams working with different instruments ______ it within a year, and the finding went into the textbooks. Choose from disputed, corroborated, overstated, hedged.
cards.a: The turn at "but two other teams … different instruments" points to outside confirmation: disputed reverses that, overstated adds a claim the sentence never makes, and hedged is dodging a position rather than testing one. The answer is corroborated.
cards.n: Independent teams plus a positive turn is the standard setup for this word.

cards.q: Because the only support for the treatment was a shoebox of letters from grateful patients, the committee called the evidence ______ and asked for a real trial. Choose from empirical, conclusive, compelling, anecdotal.
cards.a: "Letters from grateful patients" names scattered personal report: empirical would need measurement, conclusive would end the question, and compelling would not send anyone back for a trial. The answer is anecdotal.
cards.n: The clue is the kind of evidence named, not the committee's tone.

cards.q: The senator ______ that bridge inspections had been skipped for three years, though she offered no maintenance records and the department denied the charge flatly. Choose from corroborated, ascertained, alleged, elucidated.
cards.a: "No maintenance records" rules out ascertained, which requires certainty, and corroborated, which requires outside evidence; elucidated would explain something already agreed on. An accusation without proof is the fit. The answer is alleged.
cards.n: A charge plus missing proof is the signal every time.

cards.q: Faced with the new tree-ring dates, the historian ______ that his chronology was off by a decade, but argued that his account of the famine still held. Choose from conceded, asserted, discredited, presumed.
cards.a: "But argued that his account still held" marks a small surrender inside a defense: asserted would claim more, discredited would attack someone else, and presumed would assume without proof. The answer is conceded.
cards.n: The but clause shows one point given up to protect the rest.

cards.q: Rumors that the reservoir had been contaminated proved ______: the district's weekly samples, going back four years, showed nothing above the legal limit for any metal. Choose from credible, unfounded, plausible, tenable.
cards.a: Four years of clean samples is the clue: credible would have the rumor believed, plausible would leave it standing, and tenable would let it be defended. Nothing sits underneath it. The answer is unfounded.
cards.n: When a colon supplies the evidence, read past it before choosing.

cards.q: The review praised the study's methods but noted that the university's press release ______ the results, turning a modest four-point gain into a cure for the disease. Choose from conveyed, underscored, overstated, articulated.
cards.a: "Turning a modest four-point gain into a cure" is exaggeration: conveyed would only carry the results across, underscored would only stress what is there, and articulated describes clear expression, not size. The answer is overstated.
cards.n: A small number blown up into a large claim decides this one.

cards.a: To make less severe or less harmful — verb, positive. "Planting cover crops mitigated the erosion that had stripped topsoil from the hillside fields each spring."
cards.n: Mitigate works on the damage, not the cause: you mitigate a flood's effects, while preventing the flood would stop it at the source.

cards.a: To relieve or lighten, said of pain or a burden — verb, positive. "Emergency grain shipments alleviated the famine, though the underlying drought continued for two more years."
cards.n: From Latin levis, light: alleviate lifts weight off something, so it pairs with suffering, pain and burdens rather than with rules or costs.

cards.a: To weaken or thin out in force — verb, neutral. "The signal attenuates as it travels through rock, so detectors are buried close to the source."
cards.n: Attenuate is the physics word in this family: a wave, a dose or an effect loses strength, and no one's suffering is involved.

cards.a: To balance out with an opposing force — verb, neutral. "Rising export sales offset the losses from the domestic market, leaving the firm's total revenue flat."
cards.n: Offset erases nothing: both forces stay in the passage and cancel, which is why it turns up in economics tables and budget arguments.

cards.a: To make worse or more severe — verb, negative. "Draining the marshes aggravated the flooding downstream, since nothing remained to absorb the spring runoff."
cards.n: In casual speech aggravate means annoy; on the test it means worsen a condition that already existed, and it is the exact opposite of mitigate.

cards.a: To rise sharply in scale or intensity — verb, negative. "A dispute over grazing rights escalated into a decade of raids along both sides of the border."
cards.n: Escalate climbs by steps, like an escalator, so it suits conflicts, costs and demands that grow stage by stage rather than all at once.

cards.a: To increase the strength or reach of — verb, neutral. "Social networks amplified a local complaint until it reached legislators in three states within a week."
cards.n: Amplify enlarges a signal that was already there, so it is the antonym of attenuate and never a synonym for create.

cards.a: To add to something already present — verb, neutral. "The museum augmented its fossil collection with three crates of specimens donated by a retired surveyor."
cards.n: Augment builds on a base that already exists, which is why passages augment an income, a collection or a force rather than an empty start.

cards.a: To multiply rapidly in number — verb, neutral. "Once the predator disappeared, jellyfish proliferated across the bay until they clogged the intake pipes of the plant."
cards.n: Proliferate counts copies, not size: cells, weapons and start-ups proliferate, but one lake cannot proliferate, it can only grow.

cards.a: To keep going at the same level — verb, neutral. "The colony could not sustain its population once the shallow soil gave out after four harvests."
cards.n: Sustain holds a level steady over time rather than raising it, and in a second sense a court sustains an objection by upholding it.

cards.a: To rise and fall irregularly — verb, neutral. "Prices for cotton fluctuated all season, climbing after each storm report and sinking when the forecasts cleared."
cards.n: A fluctuating quantity has no net direction, so a figure that fluctuates is neither rising nor falling overall, a favorite trap in data questions.

cards.a: To become or make smaller — verb, neutral. "Each retelling diminished the general's role until the victory belonged entirely to the troops who held the ridge."
cards.n: Diminish works both ways in a sentence: returns diminish on their own, and a writer can diminish someone's achievement on purpose.

cards.a: To shrink steadily toward nothing — verb, negative. "The herd dwindled from four thousand animals to fewer than sixty in a single generation."
cards.n: Dwindle takes no object: supplies dwindle by themselves, and you cannot dwindle something the way you can diminish it.

cards.a: To decrease gradually after a peak — verb, negative. "Public enthusiasm for the canal waned once the estimated cost tripled and the route was moved north."
cards.n: The moon waxes and then wanes, so wane implies a high point already passed; it fits influence, interest and power.

cards.a: To use up a supply of — verb, negative. "Repeated planting of the same crop depleted the nitrogen in the soil within a single decade."
cards.n: Deplete needs a stock to draw down, such as reserves, aquifers or stamina, and it implies refilling will be slow.

cards.a: To stop developing or moving — verb, negative. "Wages stagnated for a decade even as the cost of housing in the region doubled."
cards.n: Stagnate is not the same as fall: a stagnant economy holds still, which is why passages pair it with a clause about others growing.

cards.a: To encourage the growth of — verb, positive. "Small grants fostered a generation of local historians who documented towns the state archives had ignored."
cards.n: Foster takes conditions and habits as objects, such as innovation, cooperation or resentment, and it is also the word for raising another's child.

cards.a: To make a process easier — verb, positive. "Standard rail gauges facilitated trade between the two regions, cutting a week from the usual shipment."
cards.n: Facilitate removes friction but does not cause the thing: a bridge facilitates travel that people already wanted to make.

cards.a: To set a change in motion — verb, neutral. "The pamphlet catalyzed a debate that had been building quietly in the colony's assemblies for years."
cards.n: Borrowed from chemistry, where a catalyst speeds a reaction without being used up, so what catalyzes is often small next to the result.

cards.a: To prod into faster action — verb, neutral. "The drought spurred farmers to dig deeper wells, a change that emptied the aquifer faster still."
cards.n: The metaphor is a rider's spur, so the push is sudden and comes from outside; as a noun it names the cause itself.

cards.a: To slow or get in the way of — verb, negative. "Heavy spring mud hindered the survey party, which covered only three miles on its best day."
cards.n: Hinder slows progress without ending it, which separates it from thwart, where the plan fails outright.

cards.a: To obstruct the movement of — verb, negative. "Silt impeded the river's flow until the channel shifted and left the port two miles inland."
cards.n: From Latin pes, foot, with the idea of shackled feet: impede suits flow, traffic, breathing and progress more than it suits people's plans.

cards.a: To cut short or restrict — verb, negative. "The council curtailed the dredging season by six weeks after biologists reported damage to the oyster beds."
cards.n: Curtail cuts the tail off something with a planned length, such as a term, a program or a budget, and it is usually deliberate.

cards.a: To hold back or smother — verb, negative. "Rigid licensing rules stifled the small workshops that had once supplied the city with cheap tools."
cards.n: Stifle starts with cutting off air, so it fits whatever needs room to live: innovation, dissent, laughter, a yawn.

cards.a: To put down or keep from appearing — verb, negative. "The ministry suppressed the report for two years, releasing it only after a court ordered the files opened."
cards.n: Suppress applies power from above, to a revolt, a finding or a feeling, while stifle is closer to smothering something as it starts.

cards.a: To defeat a plan or effort — verb, negative. "A sudden thaw thwarted the siege, turning the army's only road into a channel of mud."
cards.n: Thwart needs an intention to defeat, so you thwart an attempt, an ambition or an escape, never a river or a trend.

cards.a: Small enough to barely matter — adjective, neutral. "The new fertilizer produced only a marginal gain in yield, well within the range of ordinary variation."
cards.n: Watch the second sense: in economics marginal means at the edge of the next unit, as in the marginal cost of one more ton.

cards.a: Advancing by small steps — adjective, neutral. "Progress on the vaccine was incremental, each trial adding a little to what the last one had shown."
cards.n: Incremental describes the shape of a change, not its size, so many small steps can still add up to a large total.

cards.a: Large enough to count — adjective, neutral. "A substantial share of the harvest went back into seed, leaving the village less grain than the figures suggest."
cards.n: On the test substantial is about size, not about being real, and it is the standing opposite of marginal in answer choices.

cards.a: Extreme and far-reaching — adjective, negative. "The drastic cut in quotas closed half of the fleet's berths in a single season."
cards.n: Drastic carries alarm, so it suits emergency measures and severe declines and is wrong for a change a writer describes approvingly.

cards.a: Happening suddenly and without warning — adjective, neutral. "The layer of ash marks an abrupt end to the forest, which never returned to the valley floor."
cards.n: Abrupt is the antonym of gradual and incremental, and applied to a person it means curt rather than quick.

cards.a: To speed up the rate of — verb, neutral. "Warmer water accelerated the retreat of the glacier, which lost more ice in five years than in the previous fifty."
cards.n: Accelerate is about rate, not direction: a decline can accelerate, so the word does not promise that the numbers are going up.

cards.a: Lasting only a short time — adjective, neutral. "The spike in readings was transient, gone from the instruments before the team finished writing it down."
cards.n: Same root as transit: the thing is passing through, and as a noun a transient is a person with no fixed home.

cards.a: Fleeting, gone almost as soon as it appears — adjective, neutral. "Desert pools are ephemeral, filling after a storm and vanishing again before the next full moon."
cards.n: From Greek for lasting a day; ephemeral is more literary than transient and often carries a note of beauty or regret.

cards.a: Happening now and then, with no pattern — adjective, neutral. "Sporadic reports of the bird came from three counties, but no nest was found for another decade."
cards.n: Sporadic is scattered and irregular, while intermittent stops and starts on something closer to a rhythm.

cards.a: Stopping and starting repeatedly — adjective, neutral. "Intermittent rain fell all week, long enough each time to halt the dig but never to soak the trench."
cards.n: Built on inter plus mittere, to send between: the gaps are the point, so it is neither constant nor rare.

cards.a: Continuing steadily despite resistance — adjective, neutral. "A persistent cough sent the miners to the clinic long before the dust reached the level the law allowed."
cards.n: Persistent has two uses on the test: a symptom that will not go away, and a researcher who will not give up.

cards.a: Lasting a long time without weakening — adjective, positive. "The treaty's enduring achievement was the border itself, unchanged through two later wars and three governments."
cards.n: Enduring praises what lasts, while persistent can annoy, so the two trade places badly in a sentence about a reputation.

cards.a: Returning year after year — adjective, neutral. "Flooding at the bend was a perennial problem, expected every spring and never once solved."
cards.n: From per plus annus, through the year: a perennial plant returns each season, and a perennial question keeps coming back in an argument.

cards.a: Inactive for a time but able to revive — adjective, neutral. "The volcano had lain dormant for nine centuries, so the villages on its slopes kept no record of an eruption."
cards.n: From Latin dormire, to sleep: the thing is resting, not finished, so a dormant seed or a dormant dispute can wake up.

cards.a: Present but not yet showing — adjective, neutral. "The infection stayed latent for years, revealing itself only when the patient's immune system weakened."
cards.n: Latent differs from dormant: a dormant thing was active once, while a latent one has never surfaced at all.

cards.a: To come before in time or order — verb, neutral. "A sharp drop in insect numbers preceded the collapse of the bird population by about three years."
cards.n: Coming first is not causing: a passage that says one event preceded another has not yet claimed it produced the other.

cards.a: Coming after something else — adjective, neutral. "The first survey missed the fault line entirely; subsequent teams mapped it in a single afternoon."
cards.n: Subsequent is the far end of the order precede sets up, and subsequently is the transition word that signals the next step.

cards.a: Happening at the same time — adjective, neutral. "Two concurrent droughts, one on the plains and one in the river valley, emptied the granaries at once."
cards.n: Con plus currere, to run together: a court hands down concurrent sentences that are served together rather than one after another.

cards.a: About to happen very soon — adjective, neutral. "The tremors made an eruption seem imminent, and the observatory moved its crews off the mountain that night."
cards.n: Do not confuse imminent with eminent, meaning distinguished, or with inherent, meaning built in from the start.

cards.a: To come into view or into being — verb, neutral. "A pattern emerged once the readings from all nine stations were plotted on the same chart."
cards.n: In science passages emerge usually introduces a finding rather than a physical exit, so emerging evidence is evidence just now becoming clear.

cards.a: To reach a final high point — verb, neutral. "Years of petitions culminated in a single afternoon's vote that redrew the district's boundaries for good."
cards.n: Culminate takes in: a process culminates in its peak, so the sentence structure itself tells you the blank wants an endpoint.

cards.a: To take the place of something older — verb, neutral. "The revised map superseded the 1892 edition, which surveyors kept only for its notes on boundary stones."
cards.n: Spelled with sede, from Latin sedere, to sit: the new thing sits above the old, which is then out of date rather than destroyed.

cards.q: Because the levees were built to hold back only a modest surge, the engineers admitted that the new barrier would merely ______ the flooding rather than prevent it. Choose from aggravate, mitigate, accelerate, thwart.
cards.a: "Merely ... rather than prevent" asks for partial relief: aggravate would worsen the flooding, accelerate would speed it up, and thwart would stop it outright. Reducing damage without removing the cause is the move. The answer is mitigate.
cards.n: The pair merely and rather than sets a ceiling on how much the barrier does, which rules out both the worsening word and the total block.

cards.q: Enrollment neither climbed nor fell over the decade; it simply ______, holding within a few dozen students of the same figure while every neighboring district grew. Choose from proliferated, dwindled, escalated, stagnated.
cards.a: "Neither climbed nor fell" rules out direction: proliferated and escalated both rise, and dwindled falls. Only a word for holding flat fits a number that stays put while its neighbors grow. The answer is stagnated.
cards.n: A neither ... nor pair kills every choice that carries a direction, which leaves the one word that means no movement.

cards.q: The bloom lasted three days at most, so the researchers called the color change ______ and warned that satellite passes a week apart would miss it entirely. Choose from ephemeral, perennial, enduring, incremental.
cards.a: "Three days at most" fixes a very short life: perennial returns yearly, enduring keeps going, and incremental describes small steps rather than duration. A word for vanishing almost at once fits. The answer is ephemeral.
cards.n: A stated span of days is a duration clue, so the three choices about repetition, persistence and step size are all off the axis.

cards.q: Silt from the upstream mines settled in the channel year after year and began to ______ the current, until barges that once ran the whole river could reach only the lower landing. Choose from facilitate, amplify, impede, sustain.
cards.a: The barges lose their range, so the current is being obstructed: facilitate and sustain would help it along, and amplify would strengthen it. Only blocking explains the shortened route. The answer is impede.
cards.n: The result clause after until tells you the sign of the blank before you weigh any of the four words.

cards.q: Support for the canal ______ steadily after the cost estimates tripled, and by the third year the committee could no longer fill its seats. Choose from proliferated, culminated, waned, fluctuated.
cards.a: Empty seats mark a steady fall from an earlier high: proliferated multiplies, culminated names a peak, and fluctuated would swing both ways instead of dropping. The answer is waned.
cards.n: Steadily is doing the work here, since it rules out the up-and-down word that a careless reader picks for any changing quantity.

cards.q: Fossils of the lizard turn up in sediments ______ to the asteroid impact, which means the species survived an event long blamed for its extinction. Choose from concurrent, dormant, imminent, subsequent.
cards.a: Survival means the fossils come after: concurrent would place them at the moment of impact, dormant describes inactivity, and imminent points ahead to something not yet arrived. The answer is subsequent.
cards.n: Survived is the clue, and it fixes the order of the two events rather than their size or their duration.

cards.a: Not ready to believe without proof — adjective, neutral. "Editors were skeptical of the claim until the researchers released the raw data behind it."
cards.n: Skeptical is not cynical: a skeptic withholds belief until the evidence arrives, while a cynic assumes bad motives from the start.

cards.a: Unable to believe what one is hearing — adjective, neutral. "The witness gave an incredulous laugh when the lawyer suggested she had slept through the storm."
cards.n: Incredulous is a reaction, skeptical a habit of mind; the test uses incredulous for surprise at one claim, not a standing policy of doubt.

cards.a: Watchful because harm is possible — adjective, neutral. "Farmers were wary of the new seed, having lost a season to a hybrid that promised the same yields."
cards.n: Wary is caution with a reason behind it, and the passage usually supplies the bad experience that taught it.

cards.a: Uneasy about what is coming — adjective, negative. "She was apprehensive about the vote, though every count in the weeks before had gone her way."
cards.n: From Latin prehendere, to seize: the fear takes hold before the event, so apprehensive always looks forward, never back.

cards.a: Convinced that people act from selfish motives — adjective, negative. "His cynical account treats every reform of that decade as a bid for votes rather than a matter of principle."
cards.n: The test contrasts cynical with skeptical: the cynic has already settled on the motive, so no evidence would change his mind.

cards.a: Worn out of enthusiasm by too much experience — adjective, negative. "Even jaded reviewers, who had sat through forty premieres that season, described the performance as a surprise."
cards.n: Jaded is earned exhaustion rather than dislike: the jaded critic once cared, and the passage says what used the interest up.

cards.a: Accepting something unwelcome without further protest — adjective, negative. "The village grew resigned to the floods, rebuilding each spring without any real hope the levees would hold."
cards.n: Resigned is not content: the speaker still dislikes the outcome and has only stopped fighting it, so it often follows a failed effort.

cards.a: Pleased with things as they are and blind to the risk — adjective, negative. "Two good harvests made the council complacent, and no one reviewed the grain stores before the drought."
cards.n: Do not confuse complacent with complaisant, which means eager to please; the test wants the smug, unwatchful one, the opposite of wary.

cards.a: A feeling that something is beneath one's notice — noun, negative. "He wrote of popular novels with open disdain, refusing to grant them even the status of entertainment."
cards.n: Disdain also works as a verb meaning to refuse as unworthy, and the test likes it where a writer declines to engage at all.

cards.a: Deep scorn for something judged worthless — noun, negative. "Her contempt for the committee was plain in a letter that answered its findings in a single line."
cards.n: Contempt runs hotter than disdain: disdain turns away, while contempt stays to condemn, which is why courts punish contempt.

cards.a: Showing open mockery and disrespect — adjective, negative. "A scornful footnote dismissed the earlier translation as the work of someone who had never heard the language spoken."
cards.n: Scornful adds ridicule to contempt, so it fits when the writer laughs at a target instead of merely rejecting it.

cards.a: Treating others as inferiors while appearing to help — adjective, negative. "The guide's condescending tone, explaining the tides twice to the fishermen, emptied the hall before noon."
cards.n: Condescending is patronizing, and the giveaway in a passage is help nobody asked for, offered to people who already know.

cards.a: Treating something as not worth considering — adjective, negative. "A dismissive wave was all the proposal received, though it had taken the engineers two years to prepare."
cards.n: Dismissive names the brush-off itself, so watch for curt replies, waves and one-line rejections in the text.

cards.a: Treating a serious matter with unearned lightness — adjective, negative. "His flippant reply to a question about the death toll cost him the support of the survivors' families."
cards.n: Flippant is humor in the wrong place, the standing opposite of earnest; a witty line is flippant only when the subject deserved gravity.

cards.a: Angry at something felt to be unjust — adjective, negative. "Readers sent indignant letters after the paper printed the names of the students without their consent."
cards.n: Indignant anger claims the moral high ground, so it pairs with unfair treatment rather than with mere annoyance.

cards.a: Openly refusing to obey or yield — adjective, neutral. "Defiant to the end, the mill workers kept the gates shut for six weeks after the order to disperse."
cards.n: Defiance is resistance shown in public, so the passage names the authority being resisted; the word can be admiring or critical.

cards.t: Standing back, or taking a side
cards.a: Uninvolved and emotionally distant — adjective, neutral. "The memoir is oddly detached, describing the author's own exile in the same flat tone it uses for the weather."
cards.n: Detached marks distance from the feeling, not from the facts; a detached writer can be fully informed about the subject.

cards.t: Standing back, or taking a side
cards.a: Free of feeling, judging on the evidence — adjective, positive. "A dispassionate review of the wreck blamed the schedule rather than the crew whom the newspapers had already named."
cards.n: Dispassionate is a compliment while detached can be a fault: one praises calm judgment, the other hints at coldness.

cards.t: Standing back, or taking a side
cards.a: Not favoring either side — adjective, positive. "An impartial panel of three historians, none of them from either country, was asked to settle the boundary claim."
cards.n: Impartial is about fairness between sides, and it does not require the panel to have no opinions of its own.

cards.t: Standing back, or taking a side
cards.a: Loyal to one side and arguing for it — adjective, negative. "The pamphlet is frankly partisan, quoting the governor's supporters at length and his critics in fragments."
cards.n: The opposite of impartial, and it says nothing about whether the claims are true, only that the selection is one-sided.

cards.t: Standing back, or taking a side
cards.a: Careful and controlled in force — adjective, positive. "Her measured response to the accusation conceded two small errors and then answered the central charge point by point."
cards.n: Restraint on purpose: it appears where the writer could have raged and chose not to, which makes it the opposite of vehement.

cards.t: Standing back, or taking a side
cards.a: Plain and unexcited in manner — adjective, neutral. "The captain's log is matter-of-fact about the storm, listing the hours lost and the sails torn without a word of alarm."
cards.n: This tone reports instead of reacting, so on the test it signals the absence of emotion, not the absence of opinion.

cards.t: Standing back, or taking a side
cards.a: Offered without commitment, open to revision — adjective, neutral. "The team's conclusions are tentative, since the sample covers a single valley and one unusually wet decade."
cards.n: This word rates how firmly a claim is held, not how weak it is, and the test pairs it against emphatic and adamant.

cards.t: Standing back, or taking a side
cards.a: Worded so it can be read two ways — adjective, negative. "His equivocal endorsement praised the candidate's energy and said nothing at all about her record in office."
cards.n: From equi plus voc, equal voice: two readings speak at once, so the vagueness is deliberate rather than accidental.

cards.a: Stated with force and no room for doubt — adjective, neutral. "The surgeon general was emphatic: the warning label would carry the word cancer or it would not go out at all."
cards.n: Emphatic describes the delivery, adamant the refusal to move; a speaker can be emphatic today and change his mind tomorrow.

cards.a: Full of intense, forceful feeling — adjective, neutral. "Vehement objections from the river towns delayed the dam for a decade, though none of the petitions were ever answered."
cards.n: Vehement is heat where emphatic is firmness, so the test uses it when the passage shows temper rather than mere insistence.

cards.a: Refusing to be moved from a position — adjective, neutral. "She was adamant that the letters be published whole, rejecting every proposal to cut the passages about her brother."
cards.n: Adamant was once the name of the hardest stone, and the word still points at the will rather than at the volume.

cards.a: Written as an attack on an opposing view — adjective, negative. "The essay is polemical rather than exploratory, spending its length dismantling a rival's theory of the famine."
cards.n: From Greek polemos, war: a polemic argues to defeat, so the test sets it against balanced or exploratory writing.

cards.a: Meant to stir a strong reaction — adjective, neutral. "Her provocative claim that the plague reshaped English wages drew three book-length replies within a year."
cards.n: On the test this is usually praise for a bold idea, not an insult: to provoke here is to call forth argument.

cards.a: Intended to instruct, often heavy-handedly — adjective, negative. "The novel turns didactic in its last chapters, pausing the plot so the doctor can lecture the reader on hygiene."
cards.n: Didactic writing teaches while pedantic writing shows off, and the test uses didactic for fiction that stops to deliver a lesson.

cards.a: Fussing over small points of learning — adjective, negative. "His pedantic footnotes correct the spelling of place names while ignoring the argument the chapter is making."
cards.n: Pedantry is about display: the corrections are usually right and beside the point, which is what separates it from thorough.

cards.a: Given as a warning — adjective, neutral. "The collapse of the fishery is told as a cautionary tale, aimed at officials now setting quotas on the next coast."
cards.n: This word names the purpose of the telling, so look for a lesson aimed at the reader's future, not a verdict on the past.

cards.a: Deep respect touching on awe — noun, positive. "The biography treats the mountain with reverence, describing each ascent as a visit rather than a conquest."
cards.n: A step above admiration because awe is mixed in; the verb revere and the adjective reverent turn up in the same passages.

cards.a: Yielding respectfully to another's authority — adjective, neutral. "His deferential letters to the older astronomer never disagree outright, even where his own measurements plainly did."
cards.n: From defer, to give way: it reads as modest or as timid depending on what the passage thinks of the authority being honored.

cards.a: Serious and sincere in purpose — adjective, positive. "Her earnest appeal to the school board, read from handwritten pages, won over three members who had come to vote against it."
cards.n: The standard opposite of flippant and of ironic: the speaker means exactly what the words say, with nothing held back.

cards.a: Honest in a way that holds nothing back — adjective, positive. "The captain's candid report named his own errors first, which is why the board accepted the rest of it."
cards.n: From candere, to shine white, the root of candle; on the test it is honesty that costs the speaker something.

cards.a: Meant to soothe and win back goodwill — adjective, positive. "The governor's conciliatory speech offered the striking miners a hearing and dropped the charges filed the week before."
cards.n: It marks an attempt to end the quarrel, so on a tone question look for concessions offered after a conflict.

cards.a: Fondly longing for an earlier time — adjective, neutral. "The essay grows nostalgic over the old rail line, recalling the depot crowds and passing over the fares that emptied them."
cards.n: From Greek nostos, homecoming, plus algos, pain: the ache is built into the word, so the sweetness comes mixed with loss.

cards.a: To express grief or regret over a loss — verb, negative. "Geographers lament the drained marshes, which held floodwater that now arrives in the towns downstream."
cards.n: Lament also works as a noun for the complaint itself, and on the test it marks sorrow rather than blame.

cards.a: Grave and darkened in mood — adjective, negative. "The final chapter is somber, closing the account of the expedition with a list of the men who did not return."
cards.n: Seriousness with gloom in it: a serious tone need not be somber, and the passage usually supplies a death or a loss.

cards.a: Sullen and gloomy in a withdrawn way — adjective, negative. "He grew morose after the second failed season, answering letters in single lines and refusing to visit the site."
cards.n: Somber describes a tone while morose describes a disposition, so this word attaches to a person rather than to a passage.

cards.a: Cheerfully confident about the outcome — adjective, positive. "The engineers remained sanguine about the tunnel, though the surveys had already found water in three of the four shafts."
cards.n: Sanguine once meant ruddy, from the old theory that blood made a person hopeful; on the test it simply means optimistic.

cards.a: Overflowing with high spirits — adjective, positive. "The exuberant final movement, all brass and drums, sits oddly beside the quiet fugue that comes before it."
cards.n: From exuberare, to overflow: the energy runs past what the occasion needs, so the word can shade into too much.

cards.a: Playfully odd, following fancy rather than plan — adjective, positive. "His whimsical diagrams give each ocean current a name and a temperament, which students remember long after the lecture."
cards.n: Lightness without mockery, which is what separates it from sardonic: a whimsical writer is amused, not superior.

cards.a: Puzzled and faintly entertained — adjective, neutral. "The curator sounds bemused by the forgery, noting that the painter had signed a name that was spelled two ways."
cards.n: Bemused does not mean amused: the core of it is confusion, and the test sets it against choices meaning delighted.

cards.a: Dryly and slightly bitterly humorous — adjective, neutral. "A wry aside about the committee's fourth study of the same bridge is the only joke in the whole report."
cards.n: The word once meant twisted, and the humor still comes from a small twist; it is gentler than sardonic and never loud.

cards.a: Meaning the opposite of what is said — adjective, neutral. "His ironic praise for the efficiency of the new system arrived in a letter that had taken five weeks to reach him."
cards.n: On the test this is a gap between statement and reality, not mere coincidence, so look for a line the passage undercuts.

cards.a: Mocking in a bitter, scornful way — adjective, negative. "The diarist's sardonic entries on the relief effort count the speeches given and the sacks of grain actually delivered."
cards.n: Wry humor with contempt added, so it belongs to a speaker who finds the target both funny and beneath him.

cards.q: Having watched three previous restoration plans collapse, the council was ______ about the new proposal and asked for a funding guarantee before committing a single acre. Choose from exuberant, wary, deferential, flippant.
cards.a: Three collapsed plans and a demand for guarantees point to caution learned from experience. Exuberant is high spirits, deferential is yielding to authority, and flippant is joking where the matter is serious. The answer is wary.
cards.n: The clue is the history of failures, so the blank has to look backward at experience, not name a mood.

cards.q: Because the panel included no one from either province, its review of the boundary claim was ______, presenting both sets of maps at equal length and drawing no conclusion of its own. Choose from partisan, polemical, indignant, impartial.
cards.a: No one from either province, plus equal space for both sets of maps, rules out taking sides. Partisan argues for one side, polemical attacks a rival view, and indignant is anger at injustice. The answer is impartial.
cards.n: Equal treatment of both sides decides it; the other three all require the writer to have a stake.

cards.q: The reviewer called the footnotes ______, since they correct the spelling of every village name in the chapter while ignoring the argument the author makes about the famine. Choose from pedantic, conciliatory, sanguine, earnest.
cards.a: Tiny corrections that skip the argument are a display of small learning. Conciliatory means trying to make peace, sanguine means optimistic about an outcome, and earnest means sincerely serious. The answer is pedantic.
cards.n: Small details right and the big question untouched is the signature of this word.

cards.q: After two decades of reviewing the same four arguments about the canal, even the historians who once found the subject thrilling had grown ______ about it. Choose from apprehensive, exuberant, jaded, adamant.
cards.a: Once thrilling, now worn down by repetition, means enthusiasm used up by experience. Apprehensive is fear of what is coming, exuberant is the opposite of worn out, and adamant is refusal to budge. The answer is jaded.
cards.n: The word once does the work: interest existed and then wore away, which no other choice allows.

cards.q: The governor's speech to the striking miners dropped the charges filed that week and promised a hearing, a ______ gesture that ended the standoff within days. Choose from polemical, dismissive, conciliatory, condescending.
cards.a: Dropped charges and an offered hearing are concessions made to end a quarrel. Polemical means attacking the other side, dismissive means refusing to engage at all, and condescending means talking down. The answer is conciliatory.
cards.n: Concessions offered after a conflict point to peacemaking, not to any of the three hostile stances.

cards.q: Because the sample covered one valley across a single unusually wet decade, the authors framed their conclusions as ______, inviting later teams to test them against a wider record. Choose from emphatic, adamant, vehement, tentative.
cards.a: A one-valley sample and an invitation to retest mean the claim is held loosely. Emphatic is force in the delivery, adamant is refusal to move, and vehement is heat of feeling. The answer is tentative.
cards.n: Hedges around a claim, not the content of it, decide how firmly the writer is holding it.

cards.a: Extremely careful about small details — adjective, positive. "The botanist kept meticulous records, noting the height of every seedling to the millimeter each morning."
cards.n: The test pairs it with diligent: diligent is about steady work over time, meticulous about fussing over the details of it.

cards.a: Strict about doing what is right and exact — adjective, positive. "She was scrupulous in crediting every source, even the pamphlet she had read only once."
cards.n: From a Latin word for a small sharp stone in the shoe — the nagging worry that keeps such a person honest.

cards.a: Guided by a sense of duty to do things properly — adjective, positive. "A conscientious lab partner, he stayed late to wash the glassware no one had assigned him."
cards.n: Shares a root with conscience: the work gets done because leaving it undone would bother the person.

cards.a: Working steadily and with care — adjective, positive. "Diligent note-taking over four winters gave the surveyor a record no single expedition could have produced."
cards.n: Passages use it for persistence over time, so it sits near tenacious, while meticulous stays about detail.

cards.a: Sensibly cautious about what may go wrong — adjective, positive. "The council thought it prudent to store two years of grain before the canal was widened."
cards.n: Not the same as timid: a prudent choice is a calculated one, while a timid one is driven by fear.

cards.a: Spending very little; sparing with resources — adjective, positive. "Frugal to the point of oddity, the inventor built his first engine from parts salvaged out of a scrapyard."
cards.n: Frugal approves where stingy does not; the test uses it for people who choose thrift, not people who hoard.

cards.a: Plain and severe, without comfort or decoration — adjective, neutral. "The monastery's austere cells held a cot, a candle and nothing else a visitor could point to."
cards.n: It describes rooms, prose styles and manners as well as people, and carries no praise or blame by itself.

cards.a: Habitually avoiding work — adjective, negative. "Critics called the young heir indolent, noting that he rose at noon and left the estate's accounts untouched."
cards.n: The opposite of diligent, and the test likes it in character sketches where the narrator is quietly disapproving.

cards.a: Sluggish and short on energy — adjective, negative. "Fever left the patient lethargic, able to lift a hand but not to follow the end of a sentence."
cards.n: This is a physical state that can pass in a day, while indolent is a settled habit of character.

cards.a: Unwilling to say much about oneself — adjective, neutral. "Reticent about the war, the veteran answered questions about his farm at length and the rest in a word."
cards.n: Reticence is usually about one subject a person will not discuss; taciturn is a general shortage of words.

cards.a: Saying little by habit — adjective, neutral. "Her taciturn grandfather went whole afternoons in the shop without speaking, though he missed nothing that was said."
cards.n: Latin tacere, to be silent, also gives us tacit; the word names a temperament, not a mood on one day.

cards.a: Careful not to reveal what should stay private — adjective, positive. "The secretary was discreet, filing the minister's letters without repeating a line of them at dinner."
cards.n: Do not confuse it with discrete, which means separate; the Writing section has tested that spelling pair.

cards.a: Keeping attention away from oneself — adjective, positive. "Self-effacing to a fault, the chemist credited her assistants and left her own name off the announcement."
cards.n: Efface means to rub out, so the person is rubbing out their own part; it is the exact opposite of ostentatious.

cards.a: Talking far too much, often about trifles — adjective, negative. "A garrulous passenger filled the entire train ride with stories about his neighbor's fence."
cards.n: Unlike gregarious, it is a complaint: the trouble is the flow of words, not the liking for company.

cards.a: Fond of the company of others — adjective, positive. "Gregarious by nature, the new teacher ate lunch with a different table of students every day."
cards.n: From Latin grex, a herd, the root behind congregate; it names sociability, not skill with words.

cards.a: Pleasant and easy to get along with — adjective, positive. "The amiable innkeeper remembered every traveler's name and never seemed to tire of the same questions."
cards.n: From Latin amare, to love; amiable describes a person, while amicable describes a settlement or a parting.

cards.a: Wishing others well and acting on it — adjective, positive. "A benevolent trustee paid the tuition of a dozen students who would never learn his name."
cards.n: Bene, well, plus velle, to wish; its opposite malevolent keeps the same halves with the bad prefix.

cards.a: Acting for the good of others at cost to oneself — adjective, positive. "Her altruistic decision to donate a kidney to a stranger surprised even the surgeons."
cards.n: Science passages use it for animal behavior that helps the group while costing the individual.

cards.a: Generous, especially toward a rival — adjective, positive. "Magnanimous in victory, the general returned the captured swords and let the garrison march out."
cards.n: Magnus, great, plus animus, spirit; the test likes it just after a contest, where pettiness was available.

cards.a: Feeling something with great warmth — adjective, positive. "A fervent admirer of the poet, she had copied out every letter he wrote before he turned thirty."
cards.n: From a Latin verb for boiling, which is why a fervent speech and a heated one are the same picture.

cards.a: Filled with eager, driving commitment to a cause — adjective, neutral. "Zealous reformers pressed the bill through three sessions, refusing every compromise offered to them."
cards.n: Praise or warning depends on the sentence: zealous work is admired, a zealous crusade is usually the writer's caution.

cards.a: Feeling and showing no interest at all — adjective, negative. "Turnout fell for a decade, and editorials blamed an apathetic public that had stopped expecting change."
cards.n: A, without, plus pathos, feeling; being apathetic is having no stake, while being impartial is having no side.

cards.a: Judging by what works in practice — adjective, positive. "The pragmatic engineer dropped the elegant design once the cheaper bridge proved it could carry the load."
cards.n: History passages set it against idealistic: the pragmatist asks what can be built, not what ought to be true.

cards.a: Quick to see what is really going on — adjective, positive. "An astute reader notices that the narrator praises his brother only when other guests are listening."
cards.n: Astute is clear-eyed judgment; shrewd adds an edge of calculation, usually about money or advantage.

cards.a: Sharp in judging what will serve one's own advantage — adjective, neutral. "A shrewd negotiator, she waited until the harvest failed before naming her price for the land."
cards.n: Approval depends on context: the word praises the judgment while hinting that self-interest is steering it.

cards.a: Highly skilled at something through practice — adjective, positive. "Adept at reading tree rings, the climatologist dated the drought to within a season or two."
cards.n: It usually takes the preposition at, and the Writing section likes to test it against the look-alikes adapt and adopt.

cards.a: Able to do many different things well — adjective, positive. "A versatile musician, he moved from the orchestra pit to a jazz trio without missing a night."
cards.n: From Latin vertere, to turn, behind revert and invert: the person turns easily to a new task.

cards.a: Someone new to an activity — noun, neutral. "The guide paired each novice with a climber who had already made the ascent twice."
cards.n: Shares a root with novel and innovate, all from Latin novus, new; the test pairs it against veteran and expert.

cards.a: Clumsy and incompetent at the task — adjective, negative. "His inept handling of the negotiation left both sides angrier than they had been that morning."
cards.n: In-, not, on the same stem as apt: the person is not fitted to the job, whatever effort he brings to it.

cards.a: Lacking experience, and so too quick to believe — adjective, negative. "It was naive of the settlers to expect a harvest from soil no one had tested."
cards.n: The fault is inexperience rather than stupidity, which is why passages use it about the young or the newly arrived.

cards.a: Easily tricked into believing anything — adjective, negative. "Gullible investors handed over their savings on the strength of a pamphlet and a rented office."
cards.n: Naive covers a general inexperience; gullible is narrower and always about swallowing what someone tells you.

cards.a: Firm and unshaken in purpose — adjective, positive. "Resolute despite two failed votes, the delegates met again in the same hall the following spring."
cards.n: Resolute approves of the firmness and obstinate condemns it, so the sentence's tone decides which one fits.

cards.a: Holding on and refusing to let go — adjective, positive. "Tenacious questioning by one reporter kept the story alive for months after the others had moved on."
cards.n: From Latin tenere, to hold, behind tenant and retain; it fits grips, memories and habits as well as people.

cards.a: Refusing to change course despite good reason — adjective, negative. "Obstinate about the old route, the captain ignored two charts showing the shoals ahead."
cards.n: Stubbornness with the blame attached: the point is that argument and evidence were offered and refused.

cards.a: Changing loyalty or liking without warning — adjective, negative. "Fickle readers abandoned the magazine within a year of the change in its cover design."
cards.n: Fickle is about whom or what a person favors; erratic is about how the person behaves from hour to hour.

cards.a: Acting on sudden whim, with no reason behind it — adjective, negative. "The capricious landlord raised one tenant's rent and forgave another's for reasons nobody could follow."
cards.n: Related to caprice, a whim; older passages call weather, rulers and fortune capricious as readily as people.

cards.a: Irregular and impossible to predict — adjective, negative. "His erratic attendance, three days one week and none the next, cost him the apprenticeship."
cards.n: From Latin errare, to wander, behind error and errand: the pattern wanders off the line it should follow.

cards.a: Liable to change or erupt at any moment — adjective, negative. "The volatile crowd cheered the speaker and, within minutes, was tearing the platform apart."
cards.n: In chemistry it means quick to evaporate, and science passages use it that way, so check the subject first.

cards.a: Boldly daring, past what caution allows — adjective, neutral. "The audacious plan called for crossing the strait in winter in boats built the month before."
cards.n: Admiring or scolding by turns; the same word covers a brilliant gamble and sheer nerve in company.

cards.a: Acting suddenly, without stopping to think — adjective, negative. "One impetuous letter, written the night of the quarrel, ended a friendship of thirty years."
cards.n: Impetuous is about speed rather than courage, so an impetuous act is often one nobody ends up admiring.

cards.a: Openly disrespectful toward someone owed respect — adjective, negative. "The insolent reply to the magistrate cost the apprentice his place before the week was out."
cards.n: It needs a target with standing: plain rudeness becomes insolence when it is aimed at an authority.

cards.a: Shamelessly bold about something that should embarrass — adjective, negative. "A brazen forgery, signed in the curator's own hand, hung in the gallery for three years."
cards.n: The word once meant made of brass, and the metal's hardness is the idea behind a face that will not blush.

cards.a: Showy in a way meant to impress onlookers — adjective, negative. "The ostentatious marble staircase served a house with four rooms and a leaking roof."
cards.n: This word is about display aimed at an audience, while pretentious is about claiming a standing you have not got.

cards.a: Claiming more importance or learning than one has — adjective, negative. "His pretentious lecture quoted six philosophers and explained none of them to the freshmen listening."
cards.n: Built on pretend and pretense: the display is a claim about the self, not merely expensive taste.

cards.a: Looking down on others as beneath one — adjective, negative. "The haughty visitor spoke to the housekeeper without once turning her head toward her."
cards.n: From haut, French for high; the posture is height, which is why it sits beside arrogant and disdainful.

cards.a: Self-important, especially in speech — adjective, negative. "The pompous chairman opened a meeting about parking with ten minutes on his own distinguished career."
cards.n: Haughty shows in how a person treats other people; pompous shows in how a person talks about himself.

cards.a: Easily frightened; short on confidence — adjective, negative. "Too timid to raise her hand, she wrote the correct answer in the margin and said nothing."
cards.n: Timid is fear, and the test contrasts it with prudent, which is caution a person has actually reasoned out.

cards.a: Easily led and willing to be taught — adjective, neutral. "The docile mare stood quietly while the veterinarian worked, though she had been broken only that spring."
cards.n: From Latin docere, to teach, behind doctor and doctrine; it suits animals and pupils more than close friends.

cards.q: Though the museum's new wing cost a fortune, its ______ marble columns and gilded ceilings drew more complaints than visitors in its first season. Choose from austere, ostentatious, frugal, meticulous.
cards.a: Marble columns and gilded ceilings are display put on for an audience, so the blank is showy: austere means bare, frugal means sparing, and meticulous is about care with detail rather than expense. The answer is ostentatious.
cards.n: The decoration named in the sentence, not the cost, is what settles the blank.

cards.q: Asked about the years he spent at sea, the old carpenter grew ______, answering three questions with a single word and turning the talk back to the weather. Choose from garrulous, gregarious, reticent, insolent.
cards.a: Three questions answered in one word, then a change of subject, is holding back on a topic: garrulous and gregarious mean the opposite, and insolent would need disrespect toward an authority. The answer is reticent.
cards.n: The clue sits after the blank, in behavior that shows silence about one subject rather than silence in general.

cards.q: Her plan to cross the desert on foot struck the committee as ______, but she had mapped every well along the route and returned with the survey they wanted. Choose from inept, lethargic, prudent, audacious.
cards.a: The but-clause shows a plan that was daring and still well prepared, so the blank is bold: inept denies her skill, lethargic makes no sense of a desert crossing, and prudent would not have alarmed anyone. The answer is audacious.
cards.n: The contrast word but tells you the blank carries the committee's alarm, not the writer's verdict.

cards.q: The village elders had trusted the surveyor's figures for years, so they were ______ enough to sign a contract none of them had read past the first page. Choose from gullible, astute, shrewd, scrupulous.
cards.a: Signing an unread contract out of long habit is trusting too easily: astute and shrewd describe people who would have read it, and scrupulous is about doing right rather than about being fooled. The answer is gullible.
cards.n: The word so makes the blank the result of years of trust, which points toward trusting too far.

cards.q: For thirty years the clerk copied every ledger entry twice and checked the totals against the receipts, a ______ habit that later saved the company from ruin. Choose from indolent, erratic, meticulous, capricious.
cards.a: Copying twice and checking every total is care with small details: indolent names someone who would never do it, and erratic and capricious both mean the habit had no pattern, while this one plainly does. The answer is meticulous.
cards.n: The routine described before the blank decides it; the praise at the end only confirms the choice.

cards.q: Three committees rejected the proposal, yet the biologist submitted it a fourth time with new data, ______ in a way her colleagues had long since stopped being. Choose from fickle, tenacious, apathetic, docile.
cards.a: Submitting a fourth time after three rejections is refusing to let go: fickle would mean she kept changing course, apathetic that she had stopped caring, and docile that she accepted the committees' verdict. The answer is tenacious.
cards.n: The repeated submissions are the clue; the colleagues who gave up only sharpen the contrast.

cards.a: An observable event or fact that calls for explanation — noun, neutral. "The phenomenon appears only at dawn, when cold air settles over the warmer surface of the lake."
cards.n: The plural is phenomena, and the test scores it: one phenomenon, two phenomena, never "a phenomena."

cards.a: A testable proposed explanation — noun, neutral. "Her hypothesis was that the beetles navigate by polarized light, a claim the team could test in a darkened tank."
cards.n: A hypothesis is not a hunch and not a conclusion: it is worded so that data can prove it wrong.

cards.a: A conclusion drawn from incomplete evidence — noun, also a verb, neutral. "Without a written record, the dating of the settlement remains conjecture, however confident the guidebooks sound."
cards.n: Weaker than a hypothesis: a hypothesis is built to be tested, while conjecture is offered without the evidence to settle it.

cards.a: A factor that can change and so can be measured — noun, neutral. "The only variable the researchers allowed to change was water temperature; light, food, and tank size stayed fixed."
cards.n: As an adjective it means changeable, so check whether the sentence names a thing in a study or describes something unsteady.

cards.a: A standard used to judge something — noun, neutral. "Cost was not a criterion; the panel ranked the designs only by how little water each one would use."
cards.n: One criterion, two criteria; the test pairs the word with "benchmark" rather than with "opinion."

cards.a: A limit that restricts what can be done — noun, neutral. "The chief constraint on the survey was daylight: the divers could work only four hours before the current rose."
cards.n: The Latin root means to bind tight, which is why a constraint holds work in, while a criticism merely objects to it.

cards.a: Able to be carried out with the means at hand — adjective, positive. "Sequencing every sample was not feasible on the grant, so the team chose thirty sites at random."
cards.n: It asks whether a plan can be done at all, not whether the plan is wise or likely to work — a separate question.

cards.a: A model or framework that organizes how a field thinks — noun, neutral. "Plate tectonics became the paradigm of modern geology, and older explanations of mountain building fell away."
cards.n: It names the big frame everyone works inside, so a paradigm shift is a change of frame, not one surprising result.

cards.a: A measured tendency for two things to vary together — noun, neutral. "The study found a strong correlation between hours of sleep and scores on the memory task."
cards.n: The test's favorite trap: it licenses no claim about which thing moved the other, or whether a third thing moved both.

cards.a: The relation in which one thing produces another — noun, neutral. "Only the controlled trial could establish causation; the earlier surveys showed the two rising together and nothing more."
cards.n: Set against correlation in almost every science passage: one is what the data shows, the other is what the data rarely proves.

cards.a: The process by which something works — noun, neutral. "The drug's effect was clear from the trial, but the mechanism behind it took another decade to describe."
cards.n: In a science passage it rarely means machinery; it names the how, the step-by-step story linking a cause to its effect.
