cards.a: Strong enough to hold up under strain or scrutiny — adjective, positive. "The finding proved robust: it held in four countries, across three age groups, and under two statistical tests."
cards.n: Of a result it means the finding survives retesting, not that the effect is large — a small effect can be robust.

cards.a: To depart from a course, rule, or norm — verb, neutral. "Two of the readings deviate sharply from the rest, and the team suspects a fault in one sensor."
cards.n: From "de" plus "via," off the road; the noun deviation is what a data point does when it wanders from the average.

cards.a: The level at which an effect begins — noun, neutral. "Below a threshold of about ten degrees, the seeds do not sprout at all, however long they are watered."
cards.n: Literally the board under a door; in a passage it marks where behavior changes, so look for "once" or "below" nearby.

cards.a: To express as a definite amount — verb, neutral. "Historians can describe the famine's reach, but the records are too thin to quantify how many households it emptied."
cards.n: Often set against "describe" or "characterize": this one demands a number, not an account.

cards.a: The size or extent of something — noun, neutral. "The effect was real but small; its magnitude was a fraction of what the earlier headlines had promised."
cards.n: Passages use it to separate "is there an effect" from "how big is it," since a certain result can still be tiny.

cards.a: Changing at a steady ratio to something else — adjective, neutral. "The time a bone takes to heal is roughly proportional to its width, so the largest breaks mend slowest."
cards.n: Watch for "inversely proportional," which means one rises exactly as the other falls, reversing the usual reading.

cards.a: To adjust an instrument against a known standard — verb, neutral. "The team calibrated each thermometer against boiling water before carrying it up the mountain."
cards.n: It is used figuratively too, for tuning a response to fit conditions, which is how an argument can be carefully calibrated.

cards.a: To imitate a real process with a model — verb, neutral. "The program simulates a century of rainfall in an afternoon, letting planners see which reservoirs run dry first."
cards.n: Not a synonym for fake: here it names a legitimate method, while "feign" carries the intent to deceive.

cards.a: To build one whole out of many parts — verb, neutral. "The review synthesizes forty studies into a single estimate of the vaccine's effect on children."
cards.n: Two senses are tested: a chemist synthesizes a compound from simpler ones, and a writer synthesizes sources into one account.

cards.a: Uniform in composition throughout — adjective, neutral. "The sample was unusually homogeneous: every grain came from the same bed of volcanic ash."
cards.n: Greek "homos," same, plus "genos," kind; its partner sits one prefix away, so read the first syllable carefully.

cards.a: Made of parts that differ from one another — adjective, neutral. "A heterogeneous group of volunteers, drawn from nine cities and four decades of age, joined the second trial."
cards.n: "Hetero" means other; such a sample is often the stronger one, since a result that holds across differences travels further.

cards.a: Combined into a single total — adjective and noun, also a verb, neutral. "In the aggregate the towns grew, though six of the nine actually lost residents over the decade."
cards.n: A combined figure can hide the pattern inside it, which is exactly the point passages make when they reach for this word.

cards.a: Separate and individually distinct — adjective, neutral. "The disease moves in discrete stages, each with its own symptoms, rather than worsening steadily from the first day."
cards.n: Not discreet, which means tactful; the test also sets it against "continuous," the unbroken kind of change.

cards.a: New and unlike what came before — adjective, positive. "The bacterium uses a novel pathway to break down plastic, one no researcher had described before 2016."
cards.n: The book you read is a distraction: on the test the word almost always means new, and it praises originality.

cards.a: Spread through every part of something — adjective, negative. "Microplastics proved pervasive, turning up in rain, in tap water, and in the tissue of deep-sea fish."
cards.n: "Per" means through: such a thing has soaked through the whole, while a merely common thing just turns up often.

cards.a: Existing in something as a permanent part of it — adjective, neutral. "The method has an inherent limit: no telescope on the ground can see past the blur of the atmosphere."
cards.n: From "in" plus "haerere," to stick in; the contrast the test wants is with "imposed," something added from outside.

cards.a: Present from birth rather than learned — adjective, neutral. "The chicks' fear of hawk-shaped shadows is innate; birds raised in isolation crouch the first time they see one."
cards.n: Narrower than inherent: it is about birth, so it takes living things, and its opposite on the test is "acquired."

cards.a: A distinguishing feature of an organism or person — noun, neutral. "Coat color is a trait controlled by a single gene, which makes it easy to follow across generations."
cards.n: In biology passages it may be inherited or acquired but is always observable, which separates it from a motive or a belief.

cards.a: To show plainly, or plainly shown — verb and adjective, neutral. "The disorder does not manifest until adolescence, so early screening turns up almost nothing."
cards.n: Both parts of speech are tested: a symptom manifests, and an error can be manifest, meaning obvious to anyone looking.

cards.a: Easily affected or harmed by something — adjective, negative. "Seedlings grown in the warm room were susceptible to the mold that never touched the plants left outside."
cards.n: Its exact opposite on the test is immune, and it takes "to": a passage says susceptible to cold, never susceptible of it.

cards.a: Protected from, or unaffected by, something — adjective, positive. "Survivors of the 1918 outbreak were immune to the strain that swept through the town a decade later."
cards.n: The figurative use is tested too, as when a claim is immune to criticism, meaning nothing said against it lands.

cards.a: Lasting a long time or recurring — adjective, negative. "Chronic drought, not a single bad year, is what finally emptied the farms along the valley floor."
cards.n: From Greek "chronos," time; the test pairs it with acute, so this word is about duration, not severity.

cards.a: Sharp and severe, coming on quickly — adjective, negative. "An acute shortage followed the storm: the shelves emptied within two days and stayed bare for a week."
cards.n: It opposes chronic in medicine but "dull" everywhere else, where it means sharp, as in acute hearing or acute judgment.

cards.a: Producing a good result — adjective, positive. "Light grazing turned out to be beneficial to the meadow, clearing space for wildflowers the tall grasses had crowded out."
cards.n: Its straight opposite in a science passage is adverse, and the noun pair the test uses is benefit against harm.

cards.a: Tending to bring about a good result — adjective, positive. "Still air and steady cold are conducive to the formation of the crystals the team had come to photograph."
cards.n: It nearly always takes "to" and describes conditions, not actions: a room is conducive to study, never conducive for it.

cards.a: Best under the given conditions — adjective, positive. "The optimal depth for the sensors was six meters: shallower readings ran warm, and deeper ones lost the signal."
cards.n: It is not simply "very good": it names the single best point in a range, which is why passages pair it with a tradeoff.

cards.a: Harmless, or mild in effect — adjective, positive. "The growth proved benign, and the surgeon removed it as a precaution rather than as a treatment."
cards.n: Its medical opposite is malignant, but outside medicine it shades toward kindly, as in a benign climate or a benign ruler.

cards.a: Working against something, unfavorable — adjective, negative. "Adverse weather closed the site for three weeks, and the crew lost the last of the digging season."
cards.n: Do not confuse it with averse, which means unwilling: conditions are adverse, but a person is averse to risk.

cards.a: A very large supply — noun, positive. "The lake's abundance of insects in June explains why so many birds time their nesting to that one month."
cards.n: Ecology passages use it as a count of how many of a species are present, not merely as praise for a generous supply.

cards.a: A shortage relative to what is needed — noun, negative. "Scarcity of fresh water, not of farmland, is what limits how large the valley settlements can grow."
cards.n: It is measured against demand, so a thing can be rare without being scarce if almost nobody needs it.

cards.a: To use fully, or to use unfairly — verb, also a noun, neutral. "The moths exploit a gap in the bats' hearing, flying at a pitch their hunters cannot detect."
cards.n: Two senses, and the test checks which is meant: exploiting a resource can be neutral, while exploiting a person is not.

cards.a: Able to be kept up without using up what it depends on — adjective, positive. "A sustainable catch leaves enough breeding fish that next year's harvest can match this one."
cards.n: Its opposite on the test is not "wasteful" but "exhausting the stock": the question is whether the practice can continue.

cards.a: To tend land for crops, or to foster growth — verb, positive. "Farmers cultivated the terraces for centuries, carrying soil back uphill by hand each spring."
cards.n: The figurative use is common on the test, where a person cultivates a skill, a habit, or a useful relationship.

cards.a: To bring a wild species under human care and use — verb, neutral. "Goats were domesticated early, and herds followed people into valleys where no wild goat had lived."
cards.n: Taming one animal is not enough: the word requires generations of breeding that change the species itself.

cards.a: To produce or give way, or the amount produced — verb and noun, neutral. "The plot yielded twice as much grain after the rotation, though the soil had not been fertilized."
cards.n: Three senses show up — to produce, to give way, to surrender — and the sentence around it decides which.

cards.q: The survey showed only that ice cream sales and drowning rates rise together, which is a ______ and not proof that one produces the other. Choose from causation, correlation, constraint, criterion.
cards.a: "Rise together" plus "not proof that one produces the other" describes two things moving in step: causation is the very claim being denied, a constraint is a limit, and a criterion is a standard for judging. The answer is correlation.
cards.n: Rising together is all the weaker claim asserts, and the sentence rules out the stronger one for you.

cards.q: Because the volcanic ash all fell in a single week, the deposit is unusually ______, with grains of one age and one chemistry from top to bottom. Choose from heterogeneous, discrete, pervasive, homogeneous.
cards.a: "One age and one chemistry from top to bottom" means uniform throughout: heterogeneous says the opposite, discrete means separate and countable, and pervasive describes spread rather than sameness. The answer is homogeneous.
cards.n: The clue after the comma restates the blank, so the work is telling sameness from separateness.

cards.q: Sequencing every sample would have cost more than the entire grant, so the plan was not ______, and the team settled for thirty sites chosen at random. Choose from feasible, optimal, robust, benign.
cards.a: Cost above the whole grant is about what can be done at all: optimal would only mean less than best, robust describes a result that holds up under retesting, and benign means harmless. The answer is feasible.
cards.n: The clue is a hard limit on means, which points to possibility rather than to quality.

cards.q: The chicks crouch at a hawk-shaped shadow the first time they see one, even when raised alone, so the response appears to be ______ rather than learned. Choose from acute, adverse, innate, manifest.
cards.a: "Raised alone" and "rather than learned" point to something present from birth: acute means sharp or severe, adverse means unfavorable, and manifest means plainly shown. The answer is innate.
cards.n: The contrast phrase names the opposite, so the blank has to mean unlearned.

cards.q: Once the catch stayed under the level that lets enough fish breed, the fishery became ______, and the boats could take the same tonnage year after year. Choose from chronic, sustainable, susceptible, adverse.
cards.a: Taking the same amount year after year without exhausting the stock is the clue: chronic means long-lasting, susceptible means easily harmed, and adverse means unfavorable. The answer is sustainable.
cards.n: Two wrong choices describe harm and one describes duration; only one says the practice can continue.

cards.q: Two of the sixty temperature readings ______ sharply from the rest, and a later check found that one sensor had been mounted in direct sun. Choose from aggregate, simulate, quantify, deviate.
cards.a: "Sharply from the rest" calls for departing from a norm: aggregate would combine the readings, simulate would model them, and quantify would put a number on them. The answer is deviate.
cards.n: The preposition "from" is the giveaway, since only one of the four verbs takes it.

cards.a: Supreme authority over a territory — noun, neutral. "The treaty recognized the new nation's sovereignty, ending any claim the empire still made to govern its land."
cards.n: From a root meaning above: it names the authority with none above it, which is why passages attach it to nations rather than to officials.

cards.a: The power to govern oneself — noun, positive. "The colonies asked for autonomy in taxation, wanting to raise their own revenue without approval from a distant parliament."
cards.n: Sovereignty is a state's authority over everyone inside its borders; autonomy is freedom from control outside them, and a region can have one without the other.

cards.a: The range within which an authority may act — noun, neutral. "The court ruled that the dispute fell outside its jurisdiction and sent the case to a federal judge."
cards.n: Latin juris, law, plus dictio, speaking: the ground where a body's word is law, so it marks a boundary and not an amount of power.

cards.a: Authority to act, granted by voters or a higher body — noun, neutral. "Winning two thirds of the seats gave the party a mandate to rewrite the pension law."
cards.n: It cuts both ways: an election gives a party a mandate, while a government issues one, so let the sentence say who hands what to whom.

cards.a: A voter represented by an official — noun, neutral. "Representatives who ignored their constituents on the tariff question found angry crowds waiting at the county meeting hall."
cards.n: The other sense, a part that makes up a whole, shares the root: constituents constitute a district, and a constituent element makes up a compound.

cards.a: A small group at odds with the larger one it belongs to — noun, negative. "Within a year the party split into factions that could agree on nothing but their dislike of the governor."
cards.n: Madison's word in the Federalist Papers, so it is nearly always disapproving: it is a group the writer thinks puts its own interest first.

cards.a: An alliance of groups that stay separate — noun, neutral. "A coalition of farmers, railway workers, and shopkeepers pushed the bill through a legislature none of them could have moved alone."
cards.n: Set it against faction: a faction is one body splitting, a coalition several bodies joining while each keeps its own name.

cards.a: A ranked order of people or things — noun, neutral. "Beneath the emperor stood a strict hierarchy of officials, each one answering to the rank directly above him."
cards.n: Greek hieros, sacred, plus archein, to rule: it began as ranks of priests and now labels any pyramid, including one inside a company.

cards.a: A system of government run by departments and officials — noun, neutral. "The reform created a bureaucracy of inspectors, clerks, and record keepers to enforce rules the old system had simply announced."
cards.n: French bureau, a desk, plus -cracy, rule: rule by the desks, which is why the word carries a sting of delay even when used neutrally.

cards.a: Holding that all people are equal — adjective, positive. "The pamphlet made an egalitarian argument: no man was born to rule another, and no title could change that."
cards.n: French egal, equal: it describes a belief or a policy, not a fact, so a passage can call a proposal egalitarian while showing it failed.

cards.a: A marked difference, usually an unfair one — noun, negative. "The report measured the disparity in school funding between the two districts, one spending nearly twice as much per student."
cards.n: Latin dis plus par, equal, so literally not equal: a difference is neutral, while this word marks a gap the writer thinks matters.

cards.a: The right to vote — noun, positive. "The amendment extended suffrage to women, doubling the number of people who could cast a ballot in national elections."
cards.n: It has nothing to do with suffering; the older sense is a vote of support, which is why the movement was called woman suffrage.

cards.a: To strip of the right to vote — verb, negative. "Poll taxes and literacy tests disenfranchised thousands of voters who had cast ballots freely in the previous decade."
cards.n: The franchise is the ballot itself and dis- takes it away; this names a legal act, unlike marginalize, which custom alone can accomplish.

cards.a: To hold down by harsh, unjust power — verb, negative. "Tenant farmers were oppressed by rents so high that a good harvest still left them deeper in debt."
cards.n: Latin ob plus premere, to press against: the pressure is continuous, which is why it describes a condition of life rather than one act.

cards.a: To bring fully under control by force — verb, negative. "Three campaigns subjugated the river valleys, and the defeated towns paid tribute to the capital for a century."
cards.n: Latin sub plus jugum, yoke: to put under the yoke. Subjugating is the conquest, oppressing is what follows once the conquered are ruled.

cards.a: To set free from legal control or from slavery — verb, positive. "The proclamation emancipated enslaved people in the rebelling states, though enforcement depended on where the army actually stood."
cards.n: Latin ex plus manus, out of the hand: freedom handed over by law, so the word implies an authority that had the power to keep holding on.

cards.a: To end a law or practice completely — verb, neutral. "Parliament abolished the slave trade in 1807, but the institution itself survived in the colonies for another generation."
cards.n: Repeal cancels a particular statute; this word ends the thing itself, which is why passages abolish slavery but repeal the act allowing it.

cards.a: Having to do with farming and farmland — adjective, neutral. "The agrarian South sold cotton abroad while northern cities filled with factories, and the two economies pulled against each other."
cards.n: Latin ager, field, the same root as agriculture; it usually appears as one half of a contrast whose other half is industrial or urban.

cards.a: To build up factories and machine production — verb, neutral. "Cities that industrialized quickly drew workers from the countryside faster than they could build housing for them."
cards.n: In history passages it is the hinge: whatever a paragraph says changed, whether wages, cities or families, the cause named is usually this.

cards.a: The basic physical systems a society runs on — noun, neutral. "Roads, canals, and telegraph lines were the infrastructure that let grain from the plains reach markets on the coast."
cards.n: Latin infra, below: the structure underneath everything else, so it names the roads and the wires, never the businesses that use them.

cards.a: A raw good bought and sold in bulk — noun, neutral. "When wheat became a commodity traded in distant exchanges, a farmer's income turned on prices set far from his fields."
cards.n: The point of the word is sameness: one bushel is as good as another, which is why such goods carry a single price and brands do not.

cards.a: Sole control of a market by one seller — noun, negative. "With every competing line bought up, the company held a monopoly and could charge what it liked for shipping."
cards.n: Greek monos, single, plus polein, to sell: one seller. The tell in a passage is not size but the absence of anyone else to buy from.

cards.a: A tax on imported goods — noun, neutral. "A high tariff on foreign iron protected mills at home and raised the price of every tool a farmer bought."
cards.n: Passages use it to set regions against each other, since the tax that shields one region's factories is paid by another region's buyers.

cards.a: To support with public money — verb, neutral. "The government subsidized the railroads with land grants, paying in acres what it could not afford to pay in cash."
cards.n: Latin subsidium, reserve troops held in support: the money props up a price or an industry the market alone would not sustain.

cards.a: An amount left over beyond what is needed — noun, positive. "Two good harvests left the province with a grain surplus, which it stored against the lean years that usually followed."
cards.n: From Latin super, over, plus a root meaning more; it is the exact opposite of deficit, and passages on budgets use the pair together.

cards.a: A shortfall of money against what is owed — noun, negative. "Years of war spending left a deficit so large that the treasury borrowed from banks in three other countries."
cards.n: Latin deficere, to fail or fall short: the money runs out before the bills stop, which is why the word implies borrowing.

cards.a: A stretch of wealth and success — noun, positive. "The decade of prosperity that followed the war filled shops, raised wages, and hid the debt building underneath it."
cards.n: Watch for the turn: passages introduce it in order to cut it short, so the sentence after it often begins with but, until or yet.

cards.a: Laws, or the making of them — noun, neutral. "The session produced legislation on child labor, factory safety, and school attendance, all of it written in a single winter."
cards.n: Latin lex, law, plus latum, carried: law carried into force. It is a mass noun, so a passage says much of it, never many of them.

cards.a: To approve formally and make binding — verb, neutral. "Nine states had to ratify the document before it took effect, and the last two held out for months."
cards.n: Latin ratus, fixed or settled: the agreement already exists, and this is the vote that settles it, so it follows negotiation, never precedes it.

cards.a: To change by adding or correcting — verb, neutral. "Delegates amended the bill twice, striking one clause about apprentices and adding another on the hours children could work."
cards.n: Latin emendare, to free from fault, the root of mend: the text is repaired rather than discarded, which is what sets it against repeal.

cards.a: To cancel a law already in force — verb, neutral. "Pressure from importers led Parliament to repeal the stamp duty, and the tax disappeared before it had run a full year."
cards.n: Only a law can be the object here; a decision is reversed and a treaty is broken, so the word tells you a statute is in the sentence.

cards.a: An earlier case that guides later ones — noun, neutral. "The ruling set a precedent, and for thirty years judges in similar disputes pointed back to it rather than arguing afresh."
cards.n: Latin praecedere, to go before. Unprecedented is its negative, so a passage calling an event unprecedented is denying exactly this.

cards.a: In place only for now — adjective, neutral. "A provisional government ran the country for eight months, drafting rules it expected an elected assembly to replace."
cards.n: Same root as provide: made to supply a need until something permanent arrives, so it implies a plan to be replaced, not mere uncertainty.

cards.a: To formally withdraw from a larger body — verb, neutral. "Eleven states voted to secede, each convention declaring that the bond with the union had been dissolved."
cards.n: Latin se, apart, plus cedere, to go; the same cede sits inside concede and recede, all of them a going away from something.

cards.a: To move from one region to another to live — verb, neutral. "Half a million people migrated north in a decade, following rumors of factory work and away from failing farms."
cards.n: Emigrate is leaving and immigrate is arriving, while this word covers the whole movement, which is why it takes north rather than from.

cards.a: A people scattered far from their homeland — noun, neutral. "The famine created a diaspora whose letters and money kept villages at home alive for two more generations."
cards.n: Greek speirein, to sow, as seed is scattered; it names the scattered people rather than the act, so a passage speaks of its members.

cards.a: Native to a place from the earliest times — adjective, neutral. "Indigenous communities had farmed the valley for centuries before any surveyor drew a line across their fields."
cards.n: Latin indi, within, plus gignere, to be born: born within. It applies to plants and animals too, so a biology passage can use it of a beetle.

cards.a: To settle and take control of another people's land — verb, negative. "Companies chartered in Europe colonized the coast, building forts first and claiming the interior on maps years later."
cards.n: It joins settlement to control, which is what separates it from migrate: settlers of this kind arrive and also govern, while migrants only arrive.

cards.a: To absorb into a dominant culture — verb, neutral. "Boarding schools were built to assimilate children, replacing their languages and clothing with those of the settlers around them."
cards.n: The root is similis, alike: made like the majority. It cuts both ways, since a group can choose it or have it forced on them, so read the agent.

cards.a: To push to the edge of power or notice — verb, negative. "New voting rules marginalized tenant farmers, leaving a third of the county with no voice in its own courthouse."
cards.n: The image is the margin of a page: the group is still on it, only out at the edge, which is milder and vaguer than being barred outright.

cards.a: A connected set of beliefs about society — noun, neutral. "Two rival ideologies split the congress, one trusting the market to sort things out and the other trusting the state."
cards.n: It names the whole system a person argues from, so calling an argument ideological suggests the conclusion arrived before the evidence.

cards.a: An official teaching or stated policy — noun, neutral. "The president's doctrine warned European powers against new colonies, and later administrations cited it for a hundred years."
cards.n: Latin docere, to teach, the root of doctor: this is handed down and accepted, while an ideology is argued for and fought over.

cards.a: Calling for change at the root — adjective, neutral. "His proposal was radical: not a repair of the tax system but a plan to abandon it and start over."
cards.n: Latin radix, root, as in radish: the test is depth, not volume, so a quiet plan to rebuild a system from the bottom still counts.

cards.a: Favoring gradual reform and improvement — adjective, positive. "Progressive reformers pushed for inspections, shorter hours, and clean water, trusting careful laws to fix what a booming city had broken."
cards.n: In a US history passage it is usually capitalized and dated: the Progressive Era names the reformers of roughly 1900 to 1920, not a party today.

cards.a: A change meant to correct a fault — noun, positive. "Labor reform came slowly, one statute at a time, each closing a single abuse the newspapers had already made famous."
cards.n: Latin re plus forma, to shape again: it mends a system from inside where a radical plan would replace it, so the two mark a debate's ends.

cards.a: Following accepted custom or practice — adjective, neutral. "The conventional view held that cities grew outward from a single center, and his maps of the suburbs quietly contradicted it."
cards.n: A convention is an agreement people have drifted into, so the word says common, not correct; passages often set it up to be overturned.

cards.q: Because the two provinces could not defeat the empire separately, they formed a ______ that held together just long enough to win independence and then dissolved. Choose from faction, coalition, hierarchy, diaspora.
cards.a: Separate provinces joining against a stronger enemy is an alliance: a faction splits one body rather than joining several, a hierarchy ranks them permanently, and a diaspora is a scattered people. The answer is coalition.
cards.n: Formed a blank to win and then dissolved names a temporary partnership, which rules out any word for a standing structure.

cards.q: The new constitution promised equal rights, yet a poll tax quietly ______ the very tenant farmers whose votes the reformers had counted on to carry the next election. Choose from emancipated, ratified, subsidized, disenfranchised.
cards.a: Yet reverses the promise of equal rights, and a tax on voting acts on the ballot: emancipated would free them, ratified approves a document, and subsidized hands out money. The answer is disenfranchised.
cards.n: The turn word sets up a negative, and the object of the verb is voters, so the blank has to be the one about the ballot.

cards.q: Two straight years of heavy harvests left the granaries with a ______ large enough that the council could sell grain abroad and still feed the city through winter. Choose from surplus, deficit, monopoly, tariff.
cards.a: Selling grain abroad and still eating points to more than was needed: a deficit is a shortfall, a monopoly is control of a market, and a tariff is a tax on imports. The answer is surplus.
cards.n: Both halves of the result clause have to be paid for out of the blank, so only the word for extra fits.

cards.q: Rather than rewrite the charter, the delegates chose to ______ a single clause, changing the number of years a judge could serve and leaving everything else untouched. Choose from repeal, secede, amend, abolish.
cards.a: Changing one clause and leaving the rest is correction, not cancellation: repeal would cancel the whole law, abolish would end the practice entirely, and secede means withdrawing from a union. The answer is amend.
cards.n: Leaving everything else untouched rules out every choice that would remove text instead of editing it.

cards.q: The treaty let the territory keep its own schools, courts, and language, granting a degree of ______ that stopped well short of full independence from the crown. Choose from prosperity, autonomy, jurisdiction, suffrage.
cards.a: Running its own schools and courts while remaining under the crown is self-rule: prosperity is wealth, suffrage is the vote, and jurisdiction is the reach of one authority, not a territory's freedom. The answer is autonomy.
cards.n: Stopped well short of full independence is the limit that separates self-rule from sovereignty, so the weaker word wins.

cards.q: Although her critics called the plan ______, it asked only for slightly lower rents, leaving the land system that had produced them exactly as it stood. Choose from conventional, agrarian, provisional, radical.
cards.a: Although sets the critics' label against a mild proposal, so the blank must overstate: conventional would agree with the mildness, agrarian only means farm-related, and provisional means temporary. The answer is radical.
cards.n: The turn word makes the label wrong on purpose, so pick the choice that clashes with only slightly lower rents.

cards.a: Having to do with beauty or a particular sense of style — adjective or noun, neutral. "The architect's aesthetic favored bare concrete and wide windows over the carved stone fronts of the older campus."
cards.n: On the test aesthetic is usually a noun meaning a consistent style, not a compliment; a bleak aesthetic is still an aesthetic.

cards.a: Calling up a strong image, memory or feeling — adjective, positive. "Her descriptions of the flooded orchard are so evocative that readers report smelling the wet bark for days."
cards.n: Shares a root with evoke, from Latin vocare, to call: an evocative passage calls something up in the reader rather than stating it.

cards.a: Bright, sharp and lifelike — adjective, positive. "The witness gave so vivid an account of the fire that the jury could picture the smoke filling the stairwell."
cards.n: Vivid is about intensity of detail; evocative is about what that detail stirs up, so a vivid passage can still leave a reader unmoved.

cards.a: Clear and easy to follow — adjective, positive. "Faraday's lectures were famously lucid: farmhands and physicists left the hall understanding the same demonstration."
cards.n: From Latin lux, light; it also means clear-headed, as in a lucid interval, so check whether the writer means the prose or the mind.

cards.a: Impossible to see through or to understand — adjective, negative. "The poem's final stanza remains opaque; a century of critics has not agreed on what the drowned lamp stands for."
cards.n: The literal sense is physical, blocking light; the test uses the figurative one, the exact opposite of lucid or transparent.

cards.a: Hard to make out, or little known — adjective or verb, neutral. "Smoke obscured the mountain, and the painter recorded only an obscure gray shape where the peak should be."
cards.n: As a verb it means to hide, as an adjective little-known; a passage calling a composer obscure is placing him, not judging his music.

cards.a: The material or means an artist works in — noun, neutral. "Bronze was an unforgiving medium, so the sculptor modeled each figure in wax before a single cast was poured."
cards.n: The plural is media; in a Craft and Structure question the medium is what a work is made of, while the genre is the kind of thing it is.

cards.a: A category of work with its own conventions — noun, neutral. "The novel begins as a detective story, then abandons the genre for something closer to a family memoir."
cards.n: Test questions often turn on a work breaking the rules of its genre, so watch for conventions, expectations and departure.

cards.a: The body of works an authority treats as essential — noun, neutral. "For decades the canon of American poetry taught in schools included almost no writers from the Southwest."
cards.n: One n; a cannon is a gun. Passages about the canon are usually arguing about who was left out of it.

cards.a: The arrangement of the parts of a work — noun, neutral. "In the composition, the empty road leads the eye to the two figures the artist has pushed into the corner."
cards.n: It also names a finished piece of music or writing, so decide from the sentence whether the writer means the object or its layout.

cards.a: Stripped to the fewest elements — adjective, neutral. "The minimalist score uses three notes, repeated for twenty minutes, and asks the listener to hear the small changes."
cards.n: It names a deliberate choice, not a lack of skill or effort, and sits at the opposite pole from ornate.

cards.a: Heavily decorated — adjective, neutral. "The ornate iron gate, thick with vines and scrollwork, looked absurd in front of the plain brick farmhouse."
cards.n: It can be praise or a complaint depending on the words around it, so read the sentence's attitude before you pick a charge.

cards.a: Worked out in great detail, or to add such detail — adjective or verb, neutral. "The guild's elaborate rules ran to four hundred pages, and the master elaborated on them for an hour."
cards.n: The stress moves with the sense: e-LAB-or-it describes a thing, e-LAB-or-ate means to go into more detail about one.

cards.a: Made of many small parts fitted together — adjective, neutral. "The clockmaker's intricate gearwork filled a case no larger than a walnut and still kept time to the second."
cards.n: Intricate praises the fit of the many parts; convoluted says the same complexity has become hard to follow.

cards.a: Drawn from many different sources — adjective, neutral. "Her eclectic library held medical texts, sea charts, and a shelf of cowboy novels she refused to explain."
cards.n: From Greek eklegein, to pick out: an eclectic style is chosen from everywhere, not confused or accidental.

cards.a: Copied from earlier work and adding nothing — adjective, negative. "Critics called the second album derivative, a careful imitation of the records the band had loved in high school."
cards.n: The noun derivative is neutral in math and finance; in a passage about art the adjective is always an insult.

cards.a: Introducing something new — adjective, positive. "The company's innovative kiln fired glaze at half the usual temperature, a change potters had wanted for decades."
cards.n: From Latin novus, new; the test likes to oppose it to conventional, traditional or derivative.

cards.a: First to do something and opening the way for others — adjective, positive. "Her pioneering use of X-rays in photography gave later artists a technique no one had thought to try."
cards.n: It claims priority, being first; innovative claims only novelty, so a method can be innovative long after someone else pioneered it.

cards.a: So original that later work grows out of it — adjective, positive. "The 1962 paper was seminal: nearly every study of birdsong published since cites it in the first paragraph."
cards.n: From Latin semen, seed: it means influential, the seed of a whole field, not merely early or well known.

cards.a: A brief indirect reference to something else — noun, neutral. "The title is an allusion to a psalm, and readers who miss it lose the novel's whole argument about mercy."
cards.n: Do not confuse it with illusion, a false appearance, or with a citation: an allusion names its source nowhere.

cards.a: Public respect paid to an earlier artist — noun, positive. "The director's long tracking shot is an homage to a 1948 thriller, copied angle for angle and openly credited."
cards.n: Homage borrows on purpose and admits it; a derivative work borrows and hopes the reader does not notice.

cards.a: An imitation that exaggerates a style to make it funny — noun or verb, neutral. "His parody of the epic keeps the thundering meter but sends the hero out to buy bread."
cards.n: Parody mocks the style of one work; satire uses mockery to attack a person, an institution or an idea outside the work.

cards.a: Writing that ridicules a target to expose its faults — noun, neutral. "Swift's satire proposes a monstrous policy in a calm official voice so that readers will recoil from it."
cards.n: Satire has a target outside itself and an argument, so a main purpose question about a satire wants that target named.

cards.a: An element that recurs through a work — noun, neutral. "A three-note phrase is the opera's central motif, returning whenever the exiled queen is about to speak."
cards.n: A motif repeats inside one work; a theme is the idea the repetition builds, so a motif is evidence for a theme.

cards.a: The original model that later versions follow — noun, neutral. "The stubborn small-town sheriff has become an archetype, and every new film about one borrows the same weary walk."
cards.n: Greek arche, first, plus typos, model; a stereotype is a flattened archetype, and the test treats that second word as the insult.

cards.a: Being the purest example of a type — adjective, positive. "With its brick mills and single covered bridge, the town is the quintessential New England factory settlement."
cards.n: From quinta essentia, the fifth and purest element of medieval science: it marks the best example, not merely a typical one.

cards.a: Widely recognized and standing for something larger — adjective, positive. "The photograph of the raised flag became iconic within a week, reprinted on posters in every state."
cards.n: Iconic needs an audience that recognizes the thing; quintessential is about how purely it fits a type, famous or not.

cards.a: To be the perfect example of something — verb, neutral. "The cramped, sunless flat epitomizes the housing the report describes, and the author returns to it in every chapter."
cards.n: The noun epitome once meant a summary, and that is the sense here: one case sums up a whole class.

cards.a: To give a visible or concrete form to an idea — verb, neutral. "The courthouse was meant to embody civic order: heavy stone, a straight flight of steps, no side doors."
cards.n: Body sits inside it: an abstract idea is given a body, which is why buildings, characters and laws are said to embody values.

cards.a: To give human qualities to something not human — verb, neutral. "The poem personifies the river, letting it argue with the bridge and grumble about the weight of the boats."
cards.n: A second sense applies to people: she personified patience means she was its living example, not that she wrote a poem.

cards.a: Done openly, not hidden — adjective, neutral. "The letter contains no overt threat, but its careful mention of the man's children was read as one."
cards.n: Its opposite is covert, hidden; overt says only that something is out in the open, not that it is loud or rude.

cards.a: Offensively obvious — adjective, negative. "The second paragraph is a blatant copy of the earlier report, down to a misspelled name in the table."
cards.n: Blatant carries disapproval that overt does not, so a blatant lie is worse than an overt one, not merely a plainer one.

cards.a: Easy to notice and standing out — adjective, neutral. "The one conspicuous object in the bare room is a red chair, and every visitor describes it first."
cards.n: Watch for the phrase conspicuous by its absence, where the thing you notice is what the writer left out.

cards.a: So slight or fine that it is easily missed — adjective, positive. "The change is subtle: the second portrait shifts the sitter's hand an inch, and the whole mood cools."
cards.n: The b is silent; on the test subtle usually praises control, the opposite of heavy-handed rather than of strong.

cards.a: A small shade of difference in meaning or feeling — noun, positive. "A good translation keeps the nuance between asking and pleading, which the older version flattened into one verb."
cards.n: The adjective nuanced praises an argument that admits complications instead of choosing a side loudly.

cards.a: Stated as the reason but probably not the true one — adjective, negative. "The ostensible purpose of the voyage was trade; the orders opened at sea described a military survey."
cards.n: It always sets up a contrast, so the clause after an ostensible reason gives the real one, often after but or in fact.

cards.a: Taking words in their plain, exact sense — adjective, neutral. "She meant it in the literal sense: the floor of the cave really was paved with bones, not merely crowded."
cards.n: A question may ask whether a phrase is meant literally; the answer is usually no, or the question would not be worth asking.

cards.a: Using words to mean something other than their plain sense — adjective, neutral. "The drowning in the last chapter is figurative: the man is buried in debts, not in water."
cards.n: Metaphor, simile and personification are all figurative language, and the test calls the plain-sense opposite literal.

cards.a: Dealing with ideas rather than particular things — adjective, neutral. "The essay stays abstract for ten pages, naming no country, no year and no one who lived through the famine."
cards.n: In writing about art it means not representing recognizable objects, so an abstract painting is not a vague one.

cards.a: Able to be touched, or solid enough to point to — adjective, positive. "After three years the project had one tangible result: a footbridge that carried children over the highway."
cards.n: From Latin tangere, to touch; the test uses it for results and evidence you can point at, against abstract or theoretical.

cards.a: To show something in a picture or in words — verb, neutral. "The mural depicts the strike as a single crowded morning, with the mill gates shut behind the marchers."
cards.n: Depict reports what is shown; portray leans toward the attitude taken, which is why questions ask how an author portrays someone.

cards.a: To represent someone or something in a particular light — verb, neutral. "The biography portrays the general as a cautious administrator rather than the reckless hero of the songs."
cards.n: A portray question is asking about slant, so look for the adjectives the author chose rather than the facts reported.

cards.a: To make something into a given form or state — verb, neutral. "The artist renders wet pavement in four grays, and the flood of 1913 is rendered almost beautiful."
cards.n: Three senses turn up in passages: to depict, to translate, and to cause to become, as in rendered the argument useless.

cards.a: To call up a feeling, memory or image — verb, neutral. "The smell of tar in the opening line evokes the harbor summers the narrator spends the rest of the book denying."
cards.n: Evoke works on the reader, depict works on the page, so one detail can depict a room and evoke a childhood at once.

cards.a: To spread through every part of something — verb, neutral. "A quiet dread permeates the novel, surfacing even in the cheerful letters the sisters send from the coast."
cards.n: Literally it describes liquid or smell passing through a material, and the figurative use keeps that sense of reaching everywhere.

cards.a: To place two things side by side so the contrast shows — verb, neutral. "The chapter juxtaposes the banquet menu with the ration card, and no comment from the author is needed."
cards.n: From Latin juxta, next to; the point of a juxtaposition is always the comparison the reader is left to make.

cards.q: The museum label praises the tapestry's ______ border, where more than two hundred hand-stitched birds crowd around a single panel of plain linen at the center. Choose from minimalist, opaque, ornate, tangible.
cards.a: Two hundred birds crowded into a border is heavy decoration: minimalist means stripped bare, opaque describes what you cannot see through, and tangible only means touchable. The answer is ornate.
cards.n: The evidence for the blank comes after it, in the clause counting the birds.

cards.q: Because the composer lifted whole phrases from two earlier symphonies, reviewers dismissed his new work as ______, a careful arrangement of other people's ideas. Choose from derivative, seminal, innovative, evocative.
cards.a: Lifted phrases and other people's ideas point to copying, and dismissed sets a negative charge: seminal and innovative both praise originality, and evocative describes what a work stirs up. The answer is derivative.
cards.n: Dismissed as tells you the blank is negative before you read a single choice.

cards.q: The senator's ______ reason for visiting the plant was to inspect the safety equipment, but her staff had already booked the hall next door for a campaign rally. Choose from literal, blatant, conspicuous, ostensible.
cards.a: But and the booked rally show the stated reason was not the real one: literal means plain-sense, blatant means offensively obvious, and conspicuous only means easy to notice. The answer is ostensible.
cards.n: But is the pivot: what follows it contradicts the reason the sentence just gave.

cards.q: Every time the lighthouse appears in the novel, in a dream, on a postage stamp, in a child's drawing, the reader meets the book's central ______ again. Choose from genre, motif, medium, canon.
cards.a: One image returning in different forms is a repeating element: a genre is a category of work, a medium is the material a work is made in, and a canon is a list of essential works. The answer is motif.
cards.n: A list of the places one image turns up is the definition of the word in disguise.

cards.q: After two years of meetings the committee could point to one ______ result, a footbridge over the railway, rather than another set of recommendations that nobody had funded. Choose from abstract, figurative, tangible, opaque.
cards.a: A footbridge you can walk on is set against unfunded recommendations, so the blank means solid and real: abstract and figurative both pull away from the physical, and opaque means impossible to see through. The answer is tangible.
cards.n: Rather than sets the blank against the unfunded recommendations, so it must mean solid.

cards.q: The chapter places the king's banquet menu on one page and a laborer's ration card on the next, and critics praise how coolly it ______ the two. Choose from depicts, juxtaposes, permeates, epitomizes.
cards.a: Two documents set on facing pages for the reader to compare is placing side by side: depicts would mean only shows, permeates means spreads through, and epitomizes means serves as the perfect example. The answer is juxtaposes.
cards.n: Praise for how coolly it works means the author supplies no comment, only the pairing.

cards.q: What kind of transition does the PSAT want when the second sentence turns against the first and states something that cuts the other way?
cards.a: Contrast — however, nevertheless, conversely, in contrast, on the other hand, still, yet. "The dye held fast on wool. However, it washed out of cotton within a week."
cards.n: Students pick an addition word because the second sentence is just as detailed as the first; length is not agreement.

cards.q: What kind of transition does the PSAT want when the second sentence piles another point of the same kind onto the first?
cards.a: Addition — moreover, furthermore, in addition, likewise, similarly, besides. "The alloy resists rust. Moreover, it costs less to machine than steel does."
cards.n: Students reach for a result word because the added fact feels like an outcome, but nothing in the first sentence produced it.

cards.q: What kind of transition does the PSAT want when the second sentence states what the first sentence produced?
cards.a: Cause and effect — therefore, thus, consequently, hence, accordingly, as a result. "The river silted up by 1890. Consequently, the port town lost its shipping trade."
cards.n: Sequence is the trap: subsequently only puts two events in order and never claims that one made the other happen.

cards.q: What kind of transition does the PSAT want when the second sentence gives one case of the general claim in the first?
cards.a: Example — for example, for instance, specifically, in particular, namely. "Some mosses survive total drying. For example, one revives hours after years in a herbarium."
cards.n: Restatement is the trap: an example brings a new, narrower fact, while in other words only says the same fact again.

cards.q: What kind of transition does the PSAT want when the writer grants a point to the other side before pressing on with their own?
cards.a: Concession — admittedly, granted, to be sure. "Admittedly, the sample was small. The pattern it showed still matched three much larger studies."
cards.n: Concession is not plain contrast: the writer agrees that the conceded point is true, then limits what it proves.

cards.q: What kind of transition does the PSAT want when the second sentence places its event before, after, or alongside the first in time?
cards.a: Sequence in time — meanwhile, subsequently, previously, ultimately, finally. "The vote failed in March. Subsequently, the governor called a special session."
cards.n: The trap is reading order as cause: an event that came later is not thereby an event that was caused.

cards.q: What kind of transition does the PSAT want when the second sentence says the first one over again, more plainly or more forcefully?
cards.a: Restatement or emphasis — in other words, that is, indeed, in fact. "The colony never turned a profit. In fact, it ran at a loss every year it existed."
cards.n: Example is the trap: restatement adds no new case, it only sharpens or hardens the point already made.

cards.q: What does "however" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Plain contrast — the workhorse, turning the sentence with no concession implied. "Tin mines drew settlers to the valley. However, the ore ran out within a decade."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: However turns, moreover adds; if the second sentence agrees with the first, however is wrong however different the topic sounds.

cards.q: What does "nevertheless" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Contrast after something granted — the first sentence gives ground, and this says the outcome holds anyway. "The treaty was signed in May. Nevertheless, fighting continued along the border."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Nevertheless needs a point worth pushing against; however needs only a difference between the two sentences.

cards.q: What does "nonetheless" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Contrast in spite of what was just said — the same job as nevertheless, a shade more formal. "Funding was cut in half. The survey was completed nonetheless."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Nonetheless and nevertheless are interchangeable on the test, which will never make you choose between the two.

cards.q: What does "conversely" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Contrast by flipping — it signals the reverse case, with the terms of the first sentence turned around. "Warm water holds less oxygen. Conversely, cold streams stay richly oxygenated."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Conversely needs a true inversion; in contrast needs only a difference, so conversely fails when nothing is turned around.

cards.q: What does "in contrast" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Contrast by comparison — it sets two things side by side and marks how they differ. "Desert soils lose nitrogen quickly. In contrast, peat bogs lock it away for centuries."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: In contrast compares two subjects, while however can turn one subject against itself within a single case.

cards.q: What does "on the other hand" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Contrast of two sides — it introduces the competing view or the second half of a weighing. "Solar panels cut fuel costs. On the other hand, they demand rare metals."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: On the other hand belongs to a two-sided weighing; with no first hand on the page, the test prefers however.

cards.q: What does "whereas" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Contrast inside a sentence — a conjunction, so it joins clauses rather than opening a new sentence. "Conifers differ. The larch sheds every needle each fall, whereas the pine keeps its needles for years."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Whereas cannot stand where however stands, so a period before the blank rules it out at once.

cards.q: What does "still" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Contrast that concedes — close to nevertheless, shorter and a little more conversational. "The bridge met every code. Still, the county engineer asked for a second review."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Still also means up to now in time; in a transitions question it is the concessive still, and a comma follows it.

cards.q: What does "yet" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Contrast with surprise — it marks the second sentence as unexpected after the first. "Bees should fly badly in theory. Yet they haul loads heavier than themselves for miles."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Yet here is contrast, not time; it is no relative of subsequently even though it can elsewhere mean so far.

cards.q: What does "alternatively" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Contrast between options — it offers a second workable choice, not a denial of the first. "Cities can raise the levee. Alternatively, they can buy the floodplain and let it flood."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Alternatively needs two live options; if the second sentence rejects the first outright, however is the better fit.

cards.q: What does "moreover" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Addition with weight — the added point is meant to strengthen the case, not merely extend it. "The vaccine cut infections sharply. Moreover, it shortened illness in those infected."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Moreover pushes the same way; however would reverse the case, and the test leans on that one swap more than any other.

cards.q: What does "furthermore" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Addition that goes further — the same job as moreover, often for the last and largest point. "The dam drowned two towns. Furthermore, it cut the salmon run by ninety percent."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Furthermore and moreover are interchangeable in practice; the test sets either against a contrast word, not against each other.

cards.q: What does "in addition" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Plain addition — neutral and unemphatic, it simply puts one more item beside the first. "The grant covers salaries. In addition, it pays two years of equipment rental."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: In addition sets an item alongside; consequently would claim the second item came out of the first.

cards.q: What does "likewise" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Addition by parallel — the second sentence does the same thing for a different subject. "Copper prices rose after the strike. Likewise, zinc climbed through the summer."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Likewise needs two subjects behaving the same way, while moreover just stacks further points about one.

cards.q: What does "similarly" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Addition by resemblance — it marks the second case as like the first in the way that matters. "Coral bleaches as water warms. Similarly, kelp thins during marine heat waves."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Similarly claims likeness and conversely claims inversion; the test often builds an item out of exactly that pair.

cards.q: What does "besides" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Addition of a further reason — an extra, often clinching point, in a lighter register. "The route was long. Besides, the pass stayed snowbound until the end of June."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Besides here means in addition, not except for; the preposition is a different word doing a different job.

cards.q: What does "consequently" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Cause and effect — it names the second sentence as what followed from the first. "Tariffs tripled the price of imported dye. Consequently, mills turned to domestic suppliers."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Consequently states a result and subsequently states what merely came next; this is the most tested swap in the section.

cards.q: What does "therefore" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Cause and effect in reasoning — it marks a conclusion drawn, not just an outcome in the world. "No fossils appear above the ash. Therefore, the species died out before the eruption."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Therefore draws a conclusion from evidence, while as a result reports an event that simply happened.

cards.q: What does "thus" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Cause and effect, compressed — a formal and brief therefore, at home in science writing. "The membrane blocks large ions. Thus, only water and small solutes cross it."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Thus can also mean in this way, but a transitions question is checking the result sense every time.

cards.q: What does "hence" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Cause and effect, formal — it points from a fact to what follows, often with no verb after it. "The alloy corrodes in salt air. Hence its absence from coastal bridges."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Hence is thus in a stiffer register; despite henceforth, hence itself is never a time word on this test.

cards.q: What does "accordingly" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Cause and effect through a decision — someone acted in keeping with the first sentence. "The forecast showed a hard freeze. Accordingly, the crew covered the seedlings."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Accordingly usually wants an agent who responds, whereas consequently is fine when nobody chose anything.

cards.q: What does "as a result" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Plain cause and effect — the neutral phrase, stating an outcome with no claim about reasoning. "A fungus reached the chestnuts in 1904. As a result, four billion trees were gone by 1940."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: As a result reports what happened; therefore claims what must be true, which is a move in an argument.

cards.q: What does "for example" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Example — one case offered in support of the general claim just made. "Some seeds need fire to sprout. For example, lodgepole pine cones open only in a burn."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: For example brings a new case while in other words re-says the old one, and only one of those adds information.

cards.q: What does "for instance" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Example — the same job as for example, with no difference in force or register. "Ancient cements varied by port. For instance, Roman harbor concrete used volcanic ash."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: For instance and for example are interchangeable; the test contrasts either with a cause or contrast word instead.

cards.q: What does "specifically" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Example by narrowing — it moves from the general statement to the exact case or detail. "The ban targeted one pollutant. Specifically, it capped sulfur dioxide from coal plants."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Specifically sharpens the same claim, while for example supplies a separate case that illustrates it.

cards.q: What does "in particular" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Example by singling out — it picks the notable member of a group already named. "Several colonies protested the levy. Massachusetts in particular refused to seat the collector."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: In particular wants a group named first; specifically can narrow a single statement with no group in sight.

cards.q: What does "namely" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Example that completes — it names exactly what the first sentence left unnamed. "One crop carried the colony. Namely, tobacco, which paid for every ship that came."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Namely supplies the identity promised, so it implies a complete list; for example offers only one case of many.

cards.q: What does "admittedly" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Concession — it grants a point to the other side before the writer's own point lands. "Admittedly, the dating has a wide margin. The layers still fall in the same order."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Admittedly concedes something true, while however only announces a turn and grants nothing at all.

cards.q: What does "granted" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Concession, compact — a one-word admission that opens the sentence and expects a pushback. "Granted, the orchestra was underfunded. Its recordings from those years still sell."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: This is admittedly in fewer syllables, not the verb granted, so a comma always follows it in this use.

cards.q: What does "to be sure" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Concession, formal — it concedes the strongest objection so the argument can answer it. "To be sure, the manuscript is a copy. The copyist worked from an original now lost."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: To be sure gives ground; indeed presses a point home, so the two pull in opposite directions despite sounding alike.

cards.q: What does "regardless" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Concession waved aside — it grants the first sentence and says the outcome holds anyway. "The cost estimates were disputed for years. Regardless, the tunnel opened on schedule."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Regardless brushes the first point aside; nevertheless does the same work but leans on the conflict rather than ignoring it.

cards.q: What does "meanwhile" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Sequence in time, at once — the two sentences cover the same stretch of time. "The siege dragged into winter. Meanwhile, the fleet waited out the storms at anchor."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Meanwhile is not a contrast word even when the two events differ; what it checks is whether the timing overlaps.

cards.q: What does "subsequently" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Sequence in time, after — the second event came later, with no claim that the first caused it. "The bill passed the assembly in April. Subsequently, the senate amended it twice."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Subsequently is the classic trap for consequently: coming later is not the same as coming about because of.

cards.q: What does "previously" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Sequence in time, before — the second sentence steps back to what came earlier. "The museum bought the panel in 1958. Previously, it had hung in a parish church in Umbria."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Previously reaches backward and subsequently reaches forward; the verb tense in the second sentence usually settles it.

cards.q: What does "ultimately" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Sequence in time, at the end — it reports how a long process finally came out. "Three designs went to the committee. Ultimately, the cheapest of them was built."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Ultimately can shade toward result, but it marks the end of a sequence, so therefore is not a safe substitute.

cards.q: What does "finally" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Sequence in time, last — the last step in an order that is already running. "The wool was mordanted, then boiled with madder. Finally, the cloth was rinsed in cold water."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Finally wants earlier steps on the page; ultimately can close a process that nobody listed step by step.

cards.q: What does "in other words" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Restatement — the same claim again in plainer or sharper terms, with nothing new added. "The ice sheet lost mass every year on record. In other words, no year broke even."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: In other words re-says while for example supplies a case, so new information in the second sentence rules it out.

cards.q: What does "that is" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Restatement, compact — it defines or pins down the term the first sentence just used. "The tax fell on staples. That is, on flour, salt, and beer rather than on land."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: That is clarifies a term and namely identifies the thing itself; the test rarely forces a choice between them.

cards.q: What does "indeed" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Emphasis — it agrees with the first sentence and then raises it to a stronger version. "The winter was cold. Indeed, the harbor froze solid for the first time in a century."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: Indeed strengthens agreement where however would break it, and the test likes that pair when a second sentence sounds dramatic.

cards.q: What does "in fact" signal between two sentences?
cards.a: Emphasis by correction — it sets the record straight, usually upward. "The press called the raid a skirmish. In fact, a third of the garrison was lost that night."
cards.h: → the relationship, then a pair of sentences
cards.n: In fact often corrects an impression while indeed simply agrees harder, so check whether the first sentence understated things.

cards.q: Diatoms build their glassy shells out of silica dissolved in seawater. ______, a spring bloom ends abruptly once the surface water runs out of silica, and the cells sink into the deep. Choose from moreover, consequently, previously, in other words.
cards.a: The shells depend on dissolved silica, so running out ends the bloom: cause and effect. Moreover would add a separate point, previously would move the story backward in time, and in other words would only re-say the first sentence. The answer is consequently.
cards.n: The second sentence is the outcome of the condition named in the first, so only a result word can fit.

cards.q: By 1750 the Dutch fleet still carried more cargo than any rival in Europe. ______, its share of the Atlantic trade had been shrinking for forty years, and British ports were taking the difference. Choose from therefore, for instance, meanwhile, however.
cards.a: Fleet size and shrinking share pull against each other, so the link is contrast. Therefore would make the decline the cause of the size, for instance would turn the second sentence into an example of the first, and meanwhile would claim only overlapping time. The answer is however.
cards.n: A fact that cuts against the impression the first sentence leaves calls for a turn, not an addition.

cards.q: Early jazz recordings had to fit the three minutes a ten-inch disc allowed. ______, the long improvised choruses that filled a Chicago dance hall were cut to a single chorus in the studio. Choose from as a result, nevertheless, similarly, namely.
cards.a: The three-minute limit forced the cuts, so the second sentence is the outcome. Nevertheless would turn against the first sentence, similarly would claim a matching case elsewhere, and namely would promise to name something left unnamed. The answer is as a result.
cards.n: A hard limit in the first sentence and a change in the second is the shape of a cause and effect item.

cards.q: The 1854 cholera map showed the deaths clustered around a single street pump. ______, the city's Board of Health held that the disease spread through foul air and left the pump in service. Choose from for example, thus, nevertheless, meanwhile.
cards.a: The evidence pointed one way and the board went the other, so the sentences clash: contrast. For example would make the board an illustration of the map, thus would claim the map produced that ruling, and meanwhile would mark only shared time. The answer is nevertheless.
cards.n: When the second sentence reports a response that ignores the first, the relationship is contrast, not result.

cards.q: Not every desert plant survives drought by storing water in its tissues. ______, the ocotillo drops its leaves within days and photosynthesizes through its green bark until the next rain. Choose from in addition, for instance, ultimately, admittedly.
cards.a: The ocotillo is one case of the general claim above it, so the link is example. In addition would treat it as a separate point, ultimately would place it at the end of a sequence, and admittedly would concede ground to an opponent. The answer is for instance.
cards.n: A named species right after a general claim about a group is almost always the example relationship.

cards.q: The drought that emptied the mesa villages after 1280 was no ordinary dry spell. ______, tree rings show that no summer between 1276 and 1299 brought a normal harvest. Choose from however, therefore, in fact, finally.
cards.a: The second sentence backs the first and raises it, which is emphasis. However would reverse a claim the evidence supports, therefore would make the rings a result of the drought's severity, and finally would place this last in a series of steps. The answer is in fact.
cards.n: When the second sentence proves the first harder than expected, reach for emphasis rather than contrast.
